articles.title: Acidente na BR-156 Amapá: Motociclista morre após cair em barranco | G1
articles.standfirst: Vítima sofreu parada cardiorrespiratória após acidente neste domingo (15). Falta de sinal de celular na região dificultou comunicação, e socorro só foi acionado com o uso de internet via satélite de um morador.
articles.summary: Acidente na BR-156 Amapá resulta na morte de motociclista após queda em barranco; falta de sinal de celular exigiu uso de internet via satélite para acionar o socorro.
articles.body:
Um motociclista morreu neste domingo (15) após sair da pista e cair em um barranco na Rodovia BR-156, logo após a comunidade do Calafate, no Amapá. O atendimento à ocorrência foi realizado pelo Corpo de Bombeiros Militar do Amapá (CBM-AP).

De acordo com a corporação, a equipe foi acionada por populares que presenciaram o acidente. Ao chegarem ao trecho, motoristas que estavam no local sinalizaram para que a viatura parasse.

Conforme os indícios levantados, o condutor trafegava em alta velocidade, perdeu o controle da direção na rodovia elevada , saiu da pista e caiu na parte inferior da via.

Motociclista morre ao sair da pista em alta velocidade e cair em barranco em rodovia no Amapá. — Foto: Reprodução/Internet

Quando os bombeiros alcançaram a vítima, populares já haviam retirado o capacete do homem. Ele estava inconsciente, apresentava extrema dificuldade para respirar e emitia sons de sufocamento.

Enquanto a equipe realizava o monitoramento, o motociclista sofreu uma parada cardiorrespiratória.

Os militares iniciaram imediatamente as manobras de reanimação cardiopulmonar (RCP), realizando os procedimentos por cerca de 30 minutos.

No entanto, a vítima já apresentava pupilas dilatadas e roxeamento nas extremidades, não resistindo aos ferimentos.

Ainda segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, a falta de sinal de celular e de linha telefônica no momento do acidente dificultou o pedido de socorro.

O contato com o Centro Integrado de Operações de Defesa Social (Ciosp) só foi estabelecido após a chegada de um popular que possuía o sistema de internet via satélite Starlink em seu veículo.

Bombeiros tentaram reanimar a vítima por 30 minutos. — Foto: Reprodução/Internet

articles.title: ‘A complete reversal’: China once feared becoming roadkill for Western automakers, but a quarter-century after joining the WTO, the tables have turned
articles.summary: Long before Europe worried about Chinese cars flooding its markets, China worried Europe would destroy its auto industry.
articles.body:
There was a time when China worried about competing with European carmakers. In the years leading up to China joining the World Trade Organization in 2001, the warning that circulated in the auto industry was lang lai le : " the wolf is coming ."

The wolf was technically already inside the gates—China had worked with foreign carmakers like General Motors and Volkswagen in joint ventures since the 1980s—but joining the WTO meant giving up 100% tariffs and import quotas that shielded China's domestic car industry from competitors abroad.

But despite having to lower its trade barriers, China is now the dominant carmaker, producing over 7 million cars in the first quarter of 2026, according to the International Organization of Motor Vehicle Manufacturers. That's almost twice the production of every EU country and the U.K. combined (3.7 million) and more than the 2.6 million made in the U.S.

EVs helped put China on top, to the point where the EU and U.S. imposed tariffs on Chinese-made models because Chinese government backing of the EV industry led to surplus production that's flooding overseas markets with cheap exports. Meanwhile, weak domestic demand has forced Chinese carmakers to rely on sales abroad.

Germany, whose vaunted auto industry faces an existential threat, may mandate joint ventures with China, just like China did with Volkswagen decades earlier to protect its automakers.

"There's been a complete reversal," Eric Thun , professor of Chinese business studies at Oxford, told Fortune .

As Beijing and local governments scrambled to meet economic growth targets, China built up its auto industry so much that it now has the capacity to produce an estimated two-thirds of the world's car demand.

But when former General Motors Asia Pacific president Michael Dunne first visited China in 1986, then as a graduate student learning Mandarin, he told Fortune there "was no auto industry" yet. Just two old models ruled the streets: a boxy Soviet sedan called the GAZ-24 Volga and the Volkswagen Santana.

That same year, Beijing designated auto manufacturing as a pillar in its seventh Five Year Plan. It started inviting foreign carmakers into the country, allowing them to sell in China provided they manufacture the cars in the country and partner with a Chinese firm that owned at least half the venture.

By the late 1990s, these joint ventures accounted for more than 80% of China's domestic vehicle production, according to a 2000 Congressional Research Service Report . The idea was that China would pick up the knowledge and learn to make its own cars.

articles.title: Senator slams Commerce Secretary for flow of Nvidia AI chips to China
articles.summary: Washington Senator Maria Cantwell has taken fire at the Department of Commerce for failing to keep Nvidia’s AI technology away from China.
articles.body: Washington Senator Maria Cantwell, one of the top Democrats on the Senate commerce committee, has taken fire at the Department of Commerce (DOC) under Secretary Howard Lutnick for neglecting to enforce protections intended to keep Nvidia’s AI chips away from China. In a letter to Lutnick on Sunday, Cantwell said the DOC has “undermined America’s national security,” and that its failures “help give away America’s technology advantage in AI.” > “Despite clear authority from Congress, the Department of Commerce has allowed advanced AI chips to flow through companies with ties to the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology.” In her letter, Cantwell specifically calls out instances when the DOC reportedly didn’t heed warnings from White House and intelligence officials to restrict Megaspeed’s access to AI chips, prior to allegations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a then-Megaspeed executive suspected of being a Chinese spy. Cantwell also criticizes the DOC for allowing Alibaba and ByteDance to access Nvidia chips through overseas data centers, and extending a loophole that let restricted companies obtain American AI technology through subsidiaries. The DOC is also accused of “putting business interests ahead of national security,” with Cantwell noting that Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Lutnick and now steered by his sons, reportedly held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of Lutnick’s nomination for Commerce Secretary. The letter comes ahead of a meeting in China this Thursday between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. While Congress is looking to bolster export restrictions around AI chips, The Wall Street Journal reports that Lutnick is instead expected to unveil a new initiative that will designate Nvidia — along with companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon, and Microsoft — as an AI “national champion.” The designation reportedly aims to help these companies expand overseas and compete with Chinese technology firms by granting them expedited export licence approvals. “America cannot maintain its leadership in AI if the agency responsible for protecting that advantage fails to enforce its own controls,” Cantwell said, closing her letter. “The Administration must account for its failure to enforce these protections and take immediate action to prevent America’s most sensitive technology from strengthening our adversaries.”

articles.title: Inside Democrats’ push to rein in AI-generated political ads
articles.summary: James Talarico wearing a dress. Abdul El-Sayed laughing at messages celebrating 9/11. Mike Mazzei cheek to cheek with Hilary Clinton. Spencer Pratt fighting against Batman-world villains in postapocalyptic Los Angeles. These fake images in real political ads were part of a 2026 wave of ads produced using generative AI. Some members of the incoming Democratic…
articles.body:
James Talarico wearing a dress. Abdul El-Sayed laughing at messages celebrating 9/11. Mike Mazzei cheek to cheek with Hilary Clinton. Spencer Pratt fighting against Batman-world villains in postapocalyptic Los Angeles.

These fake images in real political ads were part of a 2026 wave of ads produced using generative AI. Some members of the incoming Democratic majorities in Congress, facing public anxiety about the rapidly expanding AI and data center industries more broadly, are determined to put up some guardrails around AI in political campaigns.

At least five bills have been introduced since March to regulate or ban the use of AI in campaign or political advertisements. The bills all tackle the issue differently: mandating disclosure of AI use, banning it altogether or simply clarifying existing regulation to include generative AI.

Regulating these ads is just one piece of the larger AI regulation puzzle Democrats on Capitol Hill are set to tackle in January. When it comes to regulating AI use in political ads, lawmakers will need to balance free speech concerns.

“We just have to make sure that we are protecting democracy from manipulative tools that could set off panic or disrupt the peaceful transfer of power in the United States,” Rep. Yvette Clarke (D-N.Y.), who recently introduced legislation on the issue, told The Hill.

A total of $137 million was spent to produce and distribute 220 AI ads during the midterm cycle, according to The Wesleyan Media Project (WMP). Twenty-seven states require disclosure of AI use and four ban it altogether — creating a patchwork of differing laws across the country.

The WMP found 81 percent of AI ads were produced by Republicans, compared with only 12 percent from Democrats. Only 27 percent of the ads, which appeared in 34 states, contained disclosure of AI use.

Clarke introduced the REAL Political Advertisements Act in October to mandate this type of disclosure. Clarke told The Hill the use of AI content in political ads spreads misinformation and disinformation and poses a threat to U.S. elections.

“I was looking at some of the chat groups I was in during the election cycle and the number of AI-generated images and the information that was being shared was so distorting, it boggled the mind,” Clarke said.

“You see enough of it, you hear enough of it and at the end of the day people can be deceived,” she added.

Also in October, Rep. Shontel Brown (D-Ohio) introduced legislation that would ban the use of AI if it “deprives or defrauds” someone of their right to vote. And earlier this year, outgoing Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) reintroduced bipartisan legislation barring “materially deceptive” AI use when it comes to federal races. Sen. Jeff Merkley (D- Ore.) introduced legislation that would ban “false AI-generated election media.”

The AI Ads Act, introduced by Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) in July, takes a completely different approach from the other bills, codifying a Federal Election Commission ruling that states AI content already falls under a statutory prohibition on “fraudulent misrepresentation.”

Sarah Binder, a senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution, said Democrats will need to build a coalition behind a single proposal — which is easier said than done.

“It’s always hard, even in a majority party, to get lawmakers to coalesce around a single version of a bill,” Binder said, adding that leadership will likely take charge and “orchestrate the direction” the caucus will take.

Aside from the logistical hurdles of getting any bill across the finish line, free speech advocates are dubious about the regulation of AI ads.

Cody Venzke, a senior staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), said the organization is generally skeptical of bills like Clarke’s that would mandate disclosure.

“What really matters for these laws is for lawmakers to ensure that they’re not burdening the political speech of your average citizen,” Venzke said, noting that this legislation would need to be narrowly tailored.

He conceded, however, that a mandated label is less likely to run afoul of the First Amendment than a full ban. Venzke said individual states have repeatedly tried to ban false political speech and have failed — a fact that could apply to the AI ads debate.

Still, Democrats are concerned about the impact of the technology on unwitting voters.

Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.), a co-sponsor on Brown’s bill, told The Hill she is worried not only that voters can be manipulated, but also that people could falsely claim authentic material they disagree with is AI. She said ads using AI should at least need to meet a disclosure requirement like the mandated disclosure of who pays for an ad.

“Minimally making sure that they have to meet the same criterion, regulations as other campaign ads is something that I am absolutely in favor of,” Grijalva said.

Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) told The Hill that if mandating disclosure is the path Democrats choose to take, disclaimers must be prominent — even if viewing the ad on a cell phone.

“I don’t want a small three second clip at the end of the video or a small disclaimer that’s hard to see if you’re viewing it on your phone,” Subramanyam said. “I would want it to be very clear to the point that the person might not even want to do it.”

Clarke said she wrote her bill with the free speech implications in mind.

The New York legislator said she has yet to speak with leadership but will “aggressively” push to get her bill passed before the 2028 presidential election cycle fully kicks off.

“We’re all entitled to free speech, but we don’t have to be susceptible to deception,” Clarke said.

articles.title: Mullin: No one getting fired over nationwide ground stop
articles.summary: Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he does not expect anyone to lose their job over the equipment failure that grounded flights nationwide Friday, as airlines grapple with widespread delays and cancellations. “Who’s getting fired over this?” Fox News correspondent Peter Doocy asked Mullin during an interview on Sunday with Fox News’…
articles.body:
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he does not expect anyone to lose their job over the equipment failure that grounded flights nationwide Friday, as airlines grapple with widespread delays and cancellations.

“Who’s getting fired over this?” Fox News correspondent Peter Doocy asked Mullin during an interview on Sunday with Fox News’ “The Sunday Briefing.”

“I don’t think anybody’s going to get fired over this,” the DHS chief responded. “This was an issue with the equipment.”

Mullin said the failure stemmed from efforts to connect newer technology to the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) decades-old communications system .

“What it appears to be is that during the process of trying to make an old, 50-year-old system, which is basically an old dial-up system, work with the new technology we have today, it’s caused problems,” he continued.

Doocy also asked the DHS secretary if there was a possibility that the outage could have instead been caused by a cyberattack tied to a foreign government or hacker who flooded routers to shut down the system.

“I don’t believe in coincidences until I’m proven wrong, and right now I’m being proved wrong,” he continued. “So, is it a possibility? Possibly.”

“I would love to point it at a bad actor because then we know who to go back and punch. But the fact is, it isn’t,” he continued. “It really appears to be with 98 percent certainty that this was … because of a 50-year-old system that we’re trying to operate in today’s world.”

The Trump administration, including President Trump, has blamed years of inadequate funding for leaving the nation’s air traffic control system reliant on outdated technology.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy pinned the outage on lawmakers, renewing the push for Congress to approve an additional $50 billion to update air traffic control infrastructure.

Duffy on Sunday said, “$12.5 billion after decades of lack of investment is not nearly enough money to fix all the problems we have in the airspace.”

He also brushed off suggestions that the department cut off ties with the contractor behind the ground stop.

The Friday outage forced the FAA to temporarily ground all U.S. flights, stranding passengers across the country and triggering thousands of delays and cancellations. Although air traffic control systems have since been restored, thousands of delays have continued to impact airline passengers days later.

As of Monday morning, there are 8,999 airline delays and 562 flight cancellations nationwide, according to FlightAware .

articles.title: Feds add more rules restricting foreign access to advanced AI chips and servers.
articles.summary:
An interim final rule released by the US Department of Commerce aims to address a loophole that let Chinese companies bypass AI chip export controls by accessing them through overseas servers.
The new rule, which comes amid Nvidia’s alleged Chinese spy scandal, also requires licenses to reexport AI chips in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.
[Link: US Moves to Limit Remote Access to Advanced AI Chips | https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-16/us-moves-to-limit-remote-access-to-advanced-ai-chips | Bloomberg]
articles.body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned. What happens next?

An interim final rule released by the US Department of Commerce aims to address a loophole that let Chinese companies bypass AI chip export controls by accessing them through overseas servers.

The new rule, which comes amid Nvidia’s alleged Chinese spy scandal , also requires licenses to reexport AI chips in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.

articles.title: America’s air traffic control system couldn’t handle a single bad router
articles.summary: A single faulty router triggered a four-hour nationwide FAA ground stop and stranded 1.5 million flyers — before contradictory briefings fueled public panic.
articles.body: Thirty minutes outside Atlanta, the pilot got on the intercom to announce that something was wrong. A communications issue with the Federal Aviation Administration was cascading across the country. The pilot didn’t offer much detail except to say that the issue might affect gate access and connecting flights. For Amanda Khera, the timing couldn’t be worse. Her family vacation to a small island off the coast of Belize had already turned into a medical scare when her 22-month-old son Rio developed a high fever and had to be rushed to a local clinic. Exhausted, they were trying to get home to Virginia Beach, Virginia, to see his pediatrician and rest in their own bed. First, they had to connect through Atlanta. “It was honestly pretty scary,” Khera said. “We didn’t know if the pilot was flying blind without any access to the control towers, or if planes would run into each other.” "“We didn’t know if the pilot was flying blind without any access to the control towers, or if planes would run into each other.”" - Amanda Khera She had every right to be scared. She didn’t know what was going on in the cockpit or on the ground. She had no idea that pilots are trained to follow strict procedures that minimize safety risks during major air traffic control outages. All she knew was that several recent incidents, including a midair collision over Reagan National Airport in 2025 that killed 67 people, have called into question the safety of America’s skies. So she spent the rest of the descent looking out the window for nearby aircraft. Her flight landed safely. But she deplaned into a terminal frozen in place. More than 600 flights out of Atlanta, including their connection to Norfolk, had been canceled. And no one knew when they would be able to take off because every flight across the United States had been grounded. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: On Friday, November 13, the nation’s air traffic control system began to fail. Around 3:15PM ET, pilots and air traffic controllers in the Midwest started reporting difficulty communicating with each other over the radio. “We’re 11,000 [feet] over Grand Rapids airport, about nine miles to the west,” said the pilot of Allegiant Flight 547, his transmission already becoming garbled. “Unable to get… contact… approach on any [frequency].” Four minutes later, controllers at Quad Cities Airport in Moline, Illinois, reported similar issues across the region. “We’re dealing with some communication issues on a larger scale than we initially anticipated,” said one. “It sounds like Chicago Approach is going ATC zero, so it might be worse than we initially thought. We thought it was just here.” With communication outages spreading around the country, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop at 3:54PM ET “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” From that moment on, no airplanes were allowed to take off in US airspace. The sudden halt surprised both pilots and controllers. “Just a heads up, we went in a national ground stop,” said a controller in Seattle. “Are you saying national as in Reagan National,” asked one United pilot, “or national in the whole country?” “Across all en route facilities, they’re having communication issues.” Like so many of the safety incidents that have plagued the air traffic control system over the last few years, this latest failure began with a fragile and outdated piece of FAA infrastructure. In this case, according to the agency, the faulty system was the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure, or FTI. Built by defense giant L3Harris in the early 2000s, FTI is the data backbone of the entire air traffic control system. It links more than 4,400 aviation facilities and carries the voice and radar data controllers rely on to keep planes separated, bridging the gap between the FAA’s legacy phone-based transmission systems and modern Internet Protocol-based ones. FTI is scheduled to be replaced in 2028. Until then, L3Harris must make incremental upgrades to keep FTI operational. "“We’re dealing with some communication issues on a larger scale than we initially anticipated.”" - Air traffic controller One of these upgrades accidentally brought down the entire system, according to The Wall Street Journal. Early in the day, L3Harris contractors replaced an old wired telephone switch with a new fiber data router at the FAA radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas. Once activated, however, the router began to flood the network with hundreds of connection attempts every second. This may have added enough extra load to the system to degrade the whole network’s performance, according to I-Hong Hou, professor of electrical and computer engineering at Texas A&M University. Hou explained that telecom networks break pieces of information — radio transmissions or radar coordinates, for example — into data packets small enough to be transmitted over the network and reassembled at the other end. “When the network is degraded, it may start to lose a small portion of packets,” Hou says. “Since you need all packets to reassemble the data feed, just dropping one out of 10 packets may cause your feed to completely stop.” Most modern communications apps are built to compensate for packet loss. FaceTime, for example, will blur the video or switch to audio-only to preserve the connection. Air traffic control doesn’t have that luxury. “Many NAS [National Air Space] applications … require a highly reliable synchronization source with exceptional stability,” according to FAA technical documentation, which warns that instability may cause widespread failure of critical systems. FAA technicians believe the El Dorado router’s repeated connection attempts created enough instability within the FTI to cut off radio and radar feeds to 17 of the FAA’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers and several Terminal Radar Approach Controls. “We sometimes call this a cascading failure, meaning that one failed device can cause nearby devices to fail, and so on,” Hou says. "“We sometimes call this a cascading failure, meaning that one failed device can cause nearby devices to fail, and so on.”" - I-Hong Hou, professor of electrical and computer engineering at Texas A&M University L3Harris’s contractors isolated the malfunctioning router and another one at a nearby radar facility in Amarillo, Texas. Once those two routers were taken offline, the network began to stabilize once again. Four and a half hours later, at 8:15PM ET, the FAA lifted the ground stop. It was the nation’s longest since 9/11, spurring airlines to cancel more than 13,000 flights and delay more than 25,000 more through the weekend, according to FlightAware. And more than 1.5 million passengers were stranded. Faulty technology created the crisis. The FAA’s hamfisted attempts to reassure the public that everything was okay made the situation worse. For six hours after the ground stop began, the FAA did not provide any public updates except for a terse, 31-word press release and a single X post. Finally, at 11:30PM ET, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a press conference to explain the day’s events. Instead of providing clarity, however, they issued confusing and sometimes even contradictory statements. Mullin opened the conference with a joke (“Welcome to Friday the 13th, right?”) before confidently declaring that “there is no cyberattack.” Instead, he appeared to blame the outage on the FAA’s modernization project. “As Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology, and that new equipment and technology was just overwhelming the older system,” said Mullin. Mullin’s remark appeared to surprise Duffy, who looked at the ground and shook his head. Mullin later walked the statement back after a reporter’s follow-up question, admitting that “there’s nothing completely certain right now.” Duffy offered more details but did not exactly give a straight answer. “Our switches and routers actually got overloaded with data, and they went down,” he said. “I shouldn’t say they went down. They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers.” “I don’t want to rule out nefarious activity,” he later added. “This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like,” Mullin concluded. “We are built to handle crisis like this.” A follow-up press conference on Saturday afternoon was equally bizarre. It started with piercing audio feedback produced by a faulty microphone, which interrupted Duffy right after he introduced Rebecca Guy, the FAA’s acting chief technology officer. [Image: US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy (left) speaks as US Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin listens at the White House after the FAA issued a rare nationwide ground stop for all departing flights after a major communications outage on November 13th, 2026. After a four-minute delay, Duffy continued with the briefing. He floated the potential that contractor “incompetence” had caused the outage. And he demanded that Congress allocate billions more dollars to the FAA so it could complete its modernization efforts — calling its existing $12.5 billion modernization budget a “partial payment.” The conferences only flamed online rumors that the outage was caused by a cyberattack or a rogue AI tied to the September rollout of the FAA’s new SMART system. (So far, no evidence has emerged for either.) The problem was compounded by an administration already struggling to command public trust. When cabinet officials offered shifting, improvised explanations from the podium, millions of anxious travelers — and even prominent allies — simply refused to take the government at its word. “Until proven otherwise, not some presser by our government, I firmly believe this was a DDOS attack,” former National Security Adviser Mike Flynn wrote on X. “This is what was being described by two smart cabinet officials who clearly did not understand the technical nature of what happened.” Khera and her family didn’t know about the political gamesmanship behind the outage — and frankly, they didn’t care. She just wanted to get out of Atlanta on something other than an airplane. After a night in one of the last available hotel rooms in Atlanta, she and her family rented a car and drove the nine hours back to Virginia Beach. They made it home late Saturday night. Because of the FAA’s mishaps, they don’t plan to fly again anytime soon. “We’ve had enough of planes,” she said. “It will take a couple months and more explanations from the FAA to make sure something like this or worse doesn’t happen again.” Correction, November 16th: L3Harris contractors replaced an old wired telephone switch with a new fiber data router at the FAA radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, not a wireless one. This story has been updated to reflect that fact.

articles.title: Supreme Court won’t review implicit bias mandate for California medical courses
articles.summary: A free-speech challenge to California’s requirement that instructors teach doctors renewing their medical licenses about implicit bias fell one vote short of earning the Supreme Court’s attention on Monday. Three conservative justices — Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch — wanted to take up the challenge. But four votes were required. Ophthalmologist Azadeh Khatibi…
articles.body:
A free-speech challenge to California’s requirement that instructors teach doctors renewing their medical licenses about implicit bias fell one vote short of earning the Supreme Court ’s attention on Monday.

Three conservative justices — Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch — wanted to take up the challenge . But four votes were required.

Ophthalmologist Azadeh Khatibi and Do No Harm, a group that combats diversity initiatives in medicine, urged the justices to get involved. They argue California is compelling instructors to speak a “contested ideological message” in violation of their First Amendment rights.

The First Amendment restricts the government from conscripting private actors to deliver its forced message, but it does not regulate the government’s own speech. The lower courts ruled the medical courses are the latter and could proceed.

“That logic fundamentally misunderstands this Court’s precedents and the Constitution. First Amendment protections do not give way simply because a State heavily regulates speech,” wrote Thomas, joined by Alito.

Gorsuch dissented separately from the duo but did not explain his reasoning.

California requires licensed physicians to complete at least 50 hours of continuing medical education (CME) every two years. The challenge concerns a requirement state lawmakers passed in 2019 mandating that all courses “contain curriculum that includes the understanding of implicit bias.”

Khatibi said she is a frequent instructor of CME courses, and the courses comply with all of California’s requirements, except for the implicit bias mandate. She implored the justices to review the lower ruling.

“That sweeping ruling erases the constitutional boundary between government and private speech, threatens the speech rights of countless professionals, and directly conflicts with this Court’s precedents limiting the government speech doctrine and protecting against compelled speech,” Khatibi’s lawyers wrote to the justices.

California urged the justices to deny the ophthalmologist’s appeal. The state said the lower rulings are consistent with Supreme Court precedent and that getting involved would “imperil” medical regulations designed to protect patient health.

“Conversely, granting review and entertaining petitioners’ constitutional theory would threaten to transform regulation of the medical profession,” officials wrote in court filings.

articles.title: Iran veteran: Troops had ‘nothing’ to protect them from drone strikes
articles.summary: Combat veteran Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom on Sunday said U.S. service members in the Middle East had “nothing” to protect them from a deadly Iranian drone strike early in the U.S.-Israeli conflict with the regime in Tehran. Ramsbottom, the deputy chief of operations for the Army Reserve’s 103rd Sustainment Command, filed a whistleblower complaint to Congress…
articles.body:
Combat veteran Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom on Sunday said U.S. service members in the Middle East had “nothing” to protect them from a deadly Iranian drone strike early in the U.S.-Israeli conflict with the regime in Tehran.

Ramsbottom, the deputy chief of operations for the Army Reserve’s 103rd Sustainment Command, filed a whistleblower complaint to Congress last week urging lawmakers to investigate why there was no “dedicated protection against one-way attack drones” ahead of the March 1 attack on the U.S. outpost Port Shuaiba in Kuwait, CBS News’s “60 Minutes” reported.

“The protection that was there was to stop car bombs and threats like that,” he told CBS News’s Norah O’Donnell. “There was nothing there designed to protect from an aerial attack.”

President Trump on Monday blasted the reporting from “60 Minutes,” touting that only two one-way drone strikes out of “between 8,000-9,000” Iranian attacks resulted in “U.S. fatalities.”

“Translation: 99.99% of Iranian missiles and drones have been shot down or, in any event, not caused U.S. deaths,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “CENTCOM defensive measures have been historically effective. No one in the World has the ability to do so well. All of this being left out of the 60 Minutes ‘report.'”

The Pentagon had not disclosed the scale of the destruction brought by the attack, with “60 Minutes” reporting its own analysis of satellite imagery and new video. The outlet reported that the Pentagon declined to answer whether the 103rd was denied adequate force protection, with the agency’s investigation into the attack having wrapped in June.

The Hill has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.

The Pentagon moved around 70 members of the 103rd to the small outpost about 65 miles from Iran. Ramsbottom told O’Donnell that it’s been referred to as a “trailer park.”

He twice raised concerns to his superiors about the outpost’s protection and told O’Donnell that he was told not to worry. He added that this was a “tactical failure,” as he was told a counter-drone system would arrive, but it never did.

Iran launched a one-way drone strike on the outpost on March 1, one day after the U.S. and Israel launched the strikes that began the conflict. The attack killed six Army Reserve members and injured around 30 others.

Joey Amor, whose wife Master Sgt. Nicole Amor was among the six service members killed in the strike, told O’Donnell that he had “nothing nice to say about the 103rd.”

“I love those soldiers. And my wife loved those soldiers,” he said. “But the command of the 103rd has handled this so poorly. And if I’m being frank, it’s –– it’s on them. They killed my wife. They killed these soldiers. And it’s not political. There are individuals in that command that made choices.”

Gold Star family members told O’Donnell in the interview that they received military honors and outreach from the Trump administration but have not learned more about what happened in the attack eight months later.

articles.title: The Fed sees a new threat to the U.S. financial system
articles.summary: A new set of concerns is emerging as Wall Street navigates an increasingly uncertain environment.
articles.body:
Artificial intelligence has jumped to the top of Wall Street's worry list. In the Federal Reserve's twice-yearly survey of financial stability risks, released on November 13, AI was named the biggest danger to the system by a wide margin, ahead of every other threat respondents listed, CNBC reported.

The concern is not limited to trading floors. CNBC also cited exit polling that found that 56% of voters said AI and data centers were a "crucial or major factor" in their vote for Congress this month. That's after Democrats spent more than $100 million on ads tying Republican opponents to Big Tech and data centers.

The Fed survey draws on market participants, economists, analysts and institutional sources, and covers the period up to October 28. Eighty-seven percent cited AI as a "salient risk," up from 50% in the spring. A correction in risk assets came next at 52%, followed by higher long-term rates at 48%, and cyberattacks and fiscal debt sustainability at 43% each, according to CNBC .

The worries fall into three buckets. "Respondents noted three distinct areas of concern," the report said, pointing to elevated equity valuations and the chance of a correction if earnings disappoint, cybersecurity risk from state actors or "frontier AI models themselves," and "risks associated with complex forms of AI-related financing."

Valuations are a big part of the story. The Fed found asset prices near the upper end of their historical ranges across most markets, noting that "broad equity valuation metrics continued to be elevated, partly driven by market enthusiasm for superintelligence,"

The borrowing behind the AI buildout has also ballooned. Debt issuance tied to advanced computing topped $680 billion by October, up from $130 billion in 2023, and made up about 31% of investment-grade debt sold by nonfinancial companies this year. Outstanding public debt linked to advanced computing is estimated at more than $1.1 trillion, and the largest bank holding companies have close to $1 trillion of exposure to big tech firms, data center developers and related lending vehicles, according to the Federal Reserve .

AI financing and stretched valuations raise the stakes

Regulators are watching how tightly that money is tied together. The report flagged "the complex interlinkages among firms engaged in the data center buildout, public credit markets, private lenders" and banks. Bank exposure to nonbank financial firms passed $2.8 trillion in the second quarter, while private credit default rates have climbed to the upper end of their historical range, American Banker reported .

articles.body:
Elon Musk has signed on to a letter calling on Nvidia’s board of directors to reinstate former CEO Jensen Huang, after the ex-Nvidia chief resigned last week amid a scandal over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Musk joined more than 170,000 signatories on the open letter, including Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.

“We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA’s best interests,” the letter reads.

It calls for Huang to be reinstated as CEO, in addition to ensuring an independent investigation and a “timely public explanation” about the board’s decision.

Huang stepped down from his role leading the AI chip giant Thursday following a series of affair scandals, including one involving a woman who U.S. officials concluded was passing information to China.

It marked a major shake-up for the chipmaker and the broader AI industry. Huang founded Nvidia in 1993 and turned it into one of the world’s most valuable companies. Its chips are crucial for powering AI development.

After Huang admitted to an affair last week, Nvidia’s board launched an investigation into the incident. The open letter underscores the probe has not yet been concluded, voicing concerns that Huang was “removed without meaningful due process.”

“Thirty-three years of leadership do not place anyone above accountability,” it continues. “But accountability requires evidence, a fair hearing, and a reasoned decision. Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice.”

The letter comes ahead of Nvidia’s third-quarter earnings call Tuesday, the first under the company’s newly named interim CEO and long-standing chief financial officer, Colette Kress.

articles.title: Why NJ’s governor thinks Republicans are trapped in an X bubble
articles.summary: In the wake of a “blue wave” election where much of the country broke for Democrats, NJ Gov. Mikie Sherrill discusses tech policy, AI, and the X bubble.
articles.body: Today I’m talking with Mikie Sherrill, who’s been New Jersey governor for just a little under a year, and you’ll hear her say her election was a preview of the huge Democratic victories in these recent midterms because she ran on the dual themes of affordability and accountability. So I wanted to ask the governor exactly how corruption became such an animating issue for voters, in an era of tech billionaires who own platforms like X and TikTok and who also now control huge swaths of local media and even national broadcast media like CBS News. You’ll hear us get into the new era of influencer politics, which plays out as social video and takes its cues from rising stars like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and how I think influence on platforms like Elon Musk’s X is starting to backfire in big ways for conservatives. --- [Image: Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. --- But the real story this election cycle might be the states. With President Donald Trump concentrating power in the executive branch, governors like Sherrill are starting to exercise their own power in ways that haven’t been tested in a long time. This runs right into tech policy and anti-AI backlash, as states around the country try to address topics like child safety and Big Tech overreach in lieu of any form of meaningful federal regulation. That’s how politicians like Sherrill have found themselves at the forefront of the data center fight, online privacy, and age verification — all topics you’ll hear us dive into here. We also dig into the Meta settlement, why Sherrill expects more Big Tech litigation, and what happens to privacy in the Flock and AI era. She had a lot of questions about the last one, and honestly, so do I. It’s a conversation I think we’re all going to be having for a while. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Governor Mikie Sherrill, you’re the governor of New Jersey. Welcome to Decoder. Well, thanks so much for having me. I really appreciate it. I’m excited to talk to you. It’s after the midterms; there’s a huge blue wave, and you’re a Democrat. I noticed. Yeah. I noticed that you were saying, “New Jersey is like the bellwether,” and you “paved the way...” This is your big quote. Tell me about that, and tell me how you’re feeling about the midterms. I’ll answer the easy question first. I feel great about the midterms. I feel absolutely fantastic about the midterms. And yeah, I was thinking about it because New Jersey has those off-year elections. So, there are very few statewide races — really only two in that cycle: New Jersey and Virginia. Right after Trump won, we started our campaign. And by right after, I mean, he won in November of 2024, and we started our campaign in November of 2024. What’s so interesting about New Jersey is that, even for a governor of this state, it’s still so retail. I don’t think a lot of other big states do as much retail, meaning I’m getting in front of thousands and thousands of people, sometimes per day, at small business stops, at diners, in their community... We have so many municipalities. I am able to go to gatherings of people up and down my state. And that means that we always have a real pulse on what’s going on very quickly. After 2024, we had to get the vibe because it was different; people were furious. They wanted movement, they wanted change, and then suddenly you have Elon Musk with a chainsaw. People are scared, they don’t like what’s happening, and they want a leader who’s going to address it. And I think what we did in that time, because we heard from everyone, is really centered on what the race was about, and it was about affordability and accountability. I know now that seems obvious... Yeah, it’s about affordability, and everyone knows that. I don’t think it was obvious in 2024 what it was all about. What was driving people? And in New Jersey, we were able to figure that out, and I think because the campaign was so incredibly successful, and we had such a huge win at the end of the day, that people then thought, oh yeah, that’s exactly the path. We’re all going to run on affordability and accountability, and that’s powerful in the Democratic Party. I think we’re at the center of our power when we’re fighting for working families, and that’s where we are right now, and I think it bodes really well for the future. One of the really surprising aspects of this last election cycle was corruption leading the polls in several places. You don’t often see people on CNBC being like, “Our poll says corruption is the number one issue in America.” I think it was number two in The Guardian poll. I feel like I can connect corruption to all the tech CEOs being at the White House all the time, and to data centers. Is that a real connection, or is that just because I happen to live in the tech bubble? So, as somebody who has worked with polling, good, bad, and everything in between, I would say, and not to sound like a broken record, we were talking about... And that corruption piece was part of the accountability, the affordability. And I was hearing about that anger at corruption on the trail, even from very small, modest businesses, tying it to Trump pocketing billions of dollars as their costs are going up. I think you’re exactly right. People are very upset at the tech billionaires, and when they’re hanging out at the White House, especially those flip-floppers. They’re all in on liberal values, and then they’re all in on Trump values. It’s just to make a buck. The reason corruption popped so much is people... It’s not just corruption; it’s the corruption that’s costing them money. It’s Trump going into this Iranian war that he can’t explain and somehow making billions of dollars. It’s Trump trying to allow Russian diesel here, as everyone else is paying higher and higher gas prices, and everyone knows that Russia is funding Iran. And oh, by the way, the oligarchs are funding the wedding of Trump’s kid. Just so much corruption, and it’s tied, I think, specifically, to people’s ideas of their pocketbook and what’s making this go up. Everyone thinks it’s because Trump’s partly on the take here. One of the things that I’ve been really thinking about is how people found out about the corruption, how they talked to each other about it, and why it became such an issue. And the reason I’m asking that way is, well, Elon Musk owns X, right? He bought a social media network. Larry Ellison and Oracle have some controlling stake in TikTok. Mark Zuckerberg owns Instagram. Skydance exists, and it owns CNN. The idea that the tech billionaires control the media, and have bought more and more of the media, was supposed to create even more of an epistemic bubble. We are going to tweet policy into reality is as much a part of Trump Two as anything, and people found out what they wanted to find out, and yet they had these conversations. I haven’t been able to figure out why; do you have a theory about that case? There was a lot of corruption that we were trying to bring to the fore that was really hard to have people connect with. I think, for example, when we had Congress block some of the most high-end semiconductor chips so that we could win some of the technological battle against China, and Trump basically got paid off by the UAE, and then suddenly the floodgates were open. So, we had seen all of this cryptocurrency and stuff going into his pocketbooks. I suspect there’s a lot we don’t even know. But your point is really a good one because we were sort of saying he’s corrupt, and people sort of felt that he was corrupt, but the specifics of it were hard to bring out or get into the public consciousness. I tend to think that the interesting thing is... And look, I was very worried. I first ran in 2018, and I started to see the misinformation that people were getting online, and how people were getting algorithms driving them into more and more extreme places. I was quite skeptical of some of this new media and what it might mean for people getting information. That is certainly one concern, but the flip side of that has become, as people have gotten used to some of that extremism and maybe started to filter it out a little bit, that there’s not much you can hide now, and I think that’s really good for democracy. So, for example, we had a problem here with our voter rolls. We discovered that the last administration had registered people who were not citizens, and they had not cleared them off the rolls. And so, we discovered this, and there were a lot of people saying, “Just put out a paragraph and just kind of duck and cover and hope it goes away. Sweep it under the rug a little bit.” And to me, that’s not accountability, that’s not what I ran on, and that’s not being a strong leader. Being a strong leader is saying, “Yeah, a problem happened, but I’ve got the solution to it, and I’m going to handle it.” And I think that breeds trust in government. The reason that I maybe felt so strongly about this was that there’s no sweeping things under the rug in that way, and I think that’s really healthy. Meaning that if I had just put a little paragraph out, then the narrative would’ve gotten out anyway. I wouldn’t have been able to tell people exactly what happened, why it happened, and what we were doing about it; it would’ve been put out in whatever way somebody else wanted it out there. And so, I think what some people aren’t realizing is: you can’t hide much from the American people. The best thing you can do, and I think this is also my view of democracy and good government, is to be accountable to people. And to come forward strongly and say, this is what happened, this is why it happened, this is how I’m fixing it. One of the things that I’m really curious about in that construction is how much of this cycle was dominated by politicians who had essentially learned the visual and social vernacular of influencers. And Zohran Mamdani here in New York City has obviously learned how to wield social media as well as any influencer. Abdul El-Sayed has learned that language. After the election, I think it was a House Oversight Committee that released what can only be described as an NBA hype reel with just the words “lawyer up” over and over again. And there’s a part of me that’s like, this is incredibly effective. This is also a totally new brand of... Chuck Schumer should not do that. He doesn’t know how to do that. You need a new generation of politicians who speak this language, and sort of wield the algorithms against their owners in a very specific way. Do you think that’s permanent? Is that just a moment in time, or is influencer politics here to stay? I think getting out on social media and being very present there feels very permanent to me. There certainly are people who do it incredibly well. But the interesting thing to me is that it’s not replicable because I think you have to be so authentic. And so, Zohran Mamdani is gifted; he’s like a social media prodigy. I think he does a great job. Don’t I wish, right? I think part of the reason I like what he does is that he comes across with a lot of humanity, a lot of empathy for people, reaching out to all different kinds of people, and it’s New York City, and it feels very authentic. But I also like that empathy piece. I think some people take from the more bravado and maybe the Oversight Committee, this idea that social media has to be real… I mean, just that you have to be kind of an asshole, and you have to get out there, and that’s how you get attention, and you’re just... And I see some people trying to do that. Look, I was in the Navy, and sometimes I curse like a sailor. I do not like to do that online. Kids are online; I’m a mom too, and I’m the governor of the state of New Jersey, so I don’t have to be crass online. I have to have, I think, some respect for the office. And there are some people who I don’t think actually use salty language in back rooms, but somehow think that if they start dropping F-bombs online, they’re going to be seen as tough on stuff. The performative nature for some people is, I think, what gets them in trouble, and I think if you are authentic... And look, I’m going to be frank here, and I’m sorry, I’m not going to have as many followers as Zohran Mamdani. I’m just not. He’s, like I said, a prodigy, or gifted. I’m going to get the information; I’m going to connect with people. There are times when things hit, because we do so much in New Jersey, and people love New Jersey, and so we have a lot of Jersey stuff we do, and people like it. Great. People here in New Jersey are addicted to the weather. Great. We sadly have a lot of weather events, so we’ll hype it up. But at the same time, I think it’s really important to connect in an authentic way. And I think sometimes what you’ve seen is people looking at influencers or others who are good, and I think during the Trump administration, there were a lot of, quite frankly, toxic male bros, and somehow they learned this lesson. And yet, as you look across the people that just won, like Talarico, Amy Acton, Rob Sand... They were great people. They were really great people. And I think those are the things that, when they come across, can be so powerful. I tend to think some of those people aren’t going to have Mamdani’s following either, but you have to be making sure that you’re talking to your electorate, and you’re the person that they elected you to be. That might have been a little rambling, but I think a lot about how you connect with people in an authentic way. I’m really curious about that connection between policy, results, and authenticity. I think with Mayor Mamdani, you can see that he’s always trying to connect the policy to the result, and he’s obviously, like you said, very gifted at it. I’ll also say, I think that Rob Sand victory video, where he recreated the Fleetwood Mac meme with the cranberry juice, is an all-time piece of political communication. I’m not sure what it communicated, other than it ruled, but there is- Sometimes you just love it. What was the one from the Mississippi senator? “Pick another protein.” I thought that was so good. Yeah, it was very good. But there’s a vernacular there, right? It’s a video vernacular. In the history of politics, like JFK is the television president, there’s a vernacular with social video that came out in this election. And I’m really glad you brought up the sort of toxic energy of the Trump bros, because they feel like an X... They’re Twitter people, and they do barbs on Twitter- Interesting. And you’re feeling like the newer ones are on, what do you say, Instagram? Is that- Yeah, they’re on Instagram; they’re video. They’re natively video in a very particular way. Right. I mean, X just feels toxic. There’s something there. Especially once Elon took it over, right? Actually, here’s my hottest take. I’m curious if you agree with this. Okay, yeah, I want to hear it. My hottest take is that this election proved that Elon’s purchase of Twitter was a failure across every dimension. Anytime you’re saying something proved Elon Musk’s something something was a failure, I’m here for you. I’m here for your hot take. Well, it’s smaller than it used to be; he’s lost users. He is not making more money than Twitter ever did. And by the way, I want to qualify this by saying criticism of Elon Musk’s Twitter is in no way praise of the previous Twitter ownership. This thing has always been a disaster. But it’s smaller than it used to be; it’s certainly not making more money, and it has lost its political influence. I don’t think Twitter or X drives the national political conversation the way it used to. And in fact, because it’s become a bubble, I think it has confused a bunch of Republican politicians. I think it has confused the tech industry. I’m wondering if you see that, right? You’re talking about how we’re in bubbles, and there’s more fragmentation, that you have to be more transparent, but I’m wondering if you see the sort of collapse of X in terms of its political influence. So, you know I’m biased, but I think this is just another reason New Jersey kind of gets it right, because there are so many people who are saying they were astroturfed. I had to learn a new term in my campaign: astroturf, meaning they thought it was grassroots, but it was really just kind of the turf. There’s this fake energy sometimes on social media that people think is where everyone is at, and you can sometimes, as a good candidate in a campaign, really create that sense that everybody agrees in some area, or build a group that is going to really push that online. And yet, if you are on the ground speaking to real people all the time, you can get a sense of whether or not social media is matching up with where people are actually at. I think time and time again, there is a sense that what is going on, especially, I would say on X, can give you this false sense of a bubble, and a false sense of where people are at. And the interesting thing… I think moving away from X can maybe change a little bit of this. I do think a lot of reporters would... It’s just easy. It’s easy to go through X and get the little blah, blah, blah and say, “This is what’s happening.” And you can really miss a lot of what’s going on if that’s... So, yes, I think the bubble can really fool people. What did you make of the JD Vance post on X distancing himself from Trump, blaming it all on the war, and then the Hegseth video where he said, “Go ahead and try to impeach me.” Because those feel like pure X, like they’re talking to one audience in a small place. What’d you make of them? If he wants to be impeached, I’m sure he can find somebody to do it. Yeah, let’s do it, let’s go. I think that bravado feels so 2024, and when you see the young men, especially, who I think were captured in... People felt like they were really in the movement, in the MAGA movement in 2024. As they are graduating, as they aren’t seeing any jobs, as they’re realizing they’re not going to be able to afford a house for many, many years, or even to be able to move out of their parents’ house, I think you are seeing a real swing away. Like it’s all fun and good if you’re at some loud rally where there’s a lot of music playing and you can be a tough guy, and you feel like that’s your team, like a sports event, but it’s not so fun and funny when you can’t get a job. And so, that feels almost very 2024 to me and kind of missing the moment. That’s what’s so interesting about social media too. I think it moves very quickly. So, you might be the darling of whatever movement you’re in, and a couple years later you sound very tone-deaf. I have one more question about the election and what it means. And I want to talk about New Jersey more specifically. Trump Two has really been dominated by an almost anti-federalism. He tried to centralize a lot of power in the federal government, and the first AI bill the House passed was a 10-year moratorium on any state-level AI policy. There was a lot of, “We’re going to take power at the federal level. We’re going to bribe the states in various ways or punish the states if they don’t do what we say.” Now you’ve got a lot of democratic power across the whole government, in a bunch of state houses, in the federal government. Do you think that’s going to swing back? Do you think we’re going to see more state-level policy? Do you think we’ll see more unification between what’s happening in all the democratic states and in Congress, or do you think we’ll see more experimentation? I was listening to a political science person suggest that because of the way the US government is set up, there’s always going to be power that moves into a vacuum. And so, you saw the president taking all this power at the federal level; Congress was totally co-opted, and he had the presidency, the cabinet, and then he had the courts. So, you really did see the power moving to the people, and you started to see the people really engage more, as led by the states. In some of the governors’ offices and the state legislatures, that’s where power started to move to stand against what Trump was doing. So I was so excited about Gina Hinojosa down in Texas. The biggest swing in my race was the Latino vote. I mean, we’re talking 18/22 points, which was a real precursor to some of that swing with the Latino vote in the other states in 2024. I just started looking around. Look, everybody’s talking about Talarico, so he’s bringing tons of people to the polls, and you have Bobby Polito, Johnny Garcia. I mean, you were seeing huge movements in their districts. Then Gina was saying, “Look, we have fielded congressional candidates in every race across the state, and so that’s going to bring people out.” I was just like, I think Gina’s got a great shot here. So, we did this big event for her three weeks before the race. Just thinking, we’ve got to get her some support here because I think she can do it. And the reason I was so excited is, if you think about it, if we have California and the California governor, the Texas governor, and we have the New York governor... Man, we have a lot of the economy of the United States of America, and we can do a lot. We are moving into the state power. So, for example, Trump said he was going to purchase Russian diesel. He has Russian diesel coming here. Now, I can’t tell you how opposed I am to that. Right, you wanted to block it at the Port Authority [of New York and New Jersey], right? Right, because they said they were coming to New Jersey. So, Russia is against Ukraine. I’m very opposed to their war against Ukraine. They are also supporting Iran, which we are currently at war with. I’m very opposed to the Iranian war, but they are killing Americans because we’re at war with them, and Russia is funding them. I mean, how can you, as the President of the United States of America, be putting money into the coffers of Russia? It is not acceptable on every single level, and it, oh, by the way, is illegal, because of laws that Congress has passed. I said, “It’s not coming into New Jersey.” But the states don’t traditionally have a lot of power here. What we did was put every port and every business on notice in New Jersey that it was illegal. We charted out why it was illegal, and what laws Congress had passed, why what Trump and Bessent said was wrong — they were wrong on the law — and then we reminded everyone that the statute of limitations runs for five years, so don’t count on not getting caught on this one. And so far, we’ve seen a couple of ships turn away; I think we’re hearing that people are becoming very concerned about this, and not interested in it. If somebody had told you that the state of New Jersey could turn back the president from importing oil into this country, you would’ve been skeptical, but that’s the kind of power states are moving into at the moment and using every tool we have. It’s not that we don’t have tools; it’s just that it’s a muscle that hasn’t been exercised in this way in a long time. So, if we look to Texas, California, New York, along with New Jersey and other states, and there’s a bunch of Democratic ones now, if we want to — and we do — protect people from the downside risks of AI, we don’t need the federal government to do that. We can act as states. We can move in these ways that I think are very powerful, and have just become, after Tuesday, a lot more powerful. Yeah, I’m fascinated by this dynamic. Me too. Especially with a heavily Democratic Congress, but then President Trump, who is threatening to veto everything. Some balance of power will shift to the states in some meaningful, potentially long-lasting way. It’s unclear exactly how that will work, but I think it will probably be the long-lasting story of this cycle. I want to ask about New Jersey then, in that context. A year, not even a year into your first term, I think state governments are very opaque to people. I think a lot of the Decoder audience could tell you every bit of Apple’s org chart, and what the CO was, and what they do, and where the supply chain is, and they have no idea how their state government works. So, I want to ask you the basic Decoder questions just to illuminate that a little bit. How is New Jersey structured? How have you structured your administration? We have structured it differently than New Jersey has ever been structured. We are a large economy; we’d be the 22nd largest economy in the world if we were a country, and yet Trenton has not operated in that way. We added a chief operating officer. So, the top three people under me, my sort of lieutenants, if you will, are the chief of staff, and that’s a very traditional role. That’s sort of the person that works on the politics of the legislature and getting legislation passed... And I’m making these faces because I served in a legislature. Sometimes you have to muscle things through legislatures, even when you’re in them. You’ve got to get the coalitions; you’ve got to kind of arm-twist to get people there. In fact, the vote getter in a legislature is called the whip, to whip people into shape, to get them to vote on your bill. That’s what the chief of staff does. She also works with the outside groups, and the grassroots groups, and the politics of it... Because if you are going to get people in your state to support legislation, you have to go communicate with them, and that’s politics, that’s getting in front of mayors and county commissioners, and talking about what this is going to do for their towns, and why it’s important. So, that’s the chief of staff. Then you have the chief counsel. Now, the chief counsel sort of looks at the legislation and makes sure it’s constitutional. Are there any technical fixes that need to happen? Or are we going to get involved as a state in some of the different state legislation, like the Meta settlement and stuff? Are we going to take on some of these challenges? So, that’s sort of your chief counsel. And then we’ve added a third person, the chief operating officer. The reason we added this person is that we just felt like the state wasn’t operating on... I come from the Navy, so on mission, meaning there were a lot of different cabinet departments, and you think of that as the federal level. So, you have the Department of Human Services, the Department of Health, the Department of Education, the Department of Transportation... I mean, what you would expect at the state level. And yet they all seem to be very siloed. They were experts operating in certain areas to do things, but if you’re going to do permitting reform, that’s going to touch on your Department of Community Affairs, your Department of Environmental Protection, your Department of Transportation. And so, they argued for license plate readers, and law enforcement used those to track these cars and the car theft problem. Not to completely end it, but to do a lot of work there, and it seemed to have a big impact. In New Jersey, there are a lot of regulations around how long information could be kept. The attorney general audits it to make sure people aren’t using it inappropriately, et cetera, but you could still see a world where people are like, “Not good enough, I’m just going to lock down my house, and I want you to remove that camera from my street.” And those are choices that communities are making right now. I get the tension. I get the desire to not have somebody in my home, or stealing my car, and if somebody’s going down my street and steals a car, that somebody can be caught, and that’s not threatening other people, et cetera. But I also don’t like my privacy being invaded. I don’t want everyone tracking what’s going on. Sure, you understand that they’re audited and there are all these rules, but we know some nefarious actor could break the rules. So, it is this tension, and it’s that constant thing. We could have a society where absolutely no one breaks the law. I’m sure with technology now we could monitor the hell out of everyone, and I think they do in places like Qatar. Qatar would have you put a little app on your phone for FIFA, because we were studying all this when I was in Congress, and I was told by them, “Don’t put that app on your phone...” I didn’t go to FIFA there, but I was there to talk about one of our bases. And they said, “Don’t put that app on your phone because that’s just surveillance.” They were telling me that you can’t use your phone in your car, and if you pick up your phone, you just get a ticket because there’s that level of surveillance. Then they pointed out all the cameras to me. That is not the surveillance state I would want to live in. So, it’s going on, and there is that tension: how much is too much? Who’s getting access to the data? That was already a problem. And now it’s not a who; it’s a what. What’s AI going to do with this data? Right. If you link all the license plate readers together with an AI system, you can track anyone anywhere. We have supercharged the surveillance capability. That’s the thing that I’m just keyed on here at the end of this conversation because it is laced through everything else. Everybody has had a camera on their cell phone for over a decade now, but taking all that video, putting it together through an AI system to synthesize some new reality was not a capability we had before. We didn’t have cameras on glasses, and now we have them. And again, Mark Zuckerberg’s argument is, “Phones don’t have a light,” but that means something different to people when you’re passively recording them from your glasses. And I’m just wondering, that balance of privacy, for so long, has landed at: you don’t have an expectation of privacy in public. That is the state of the law. But you add a bunch of cameras and AI to that system, and I think people are pushing back against that law. Culturally, that expectation is changing. I should have some privacy in public. Right. I was just thinking, though, what’s so interesting to me is, as you were talking about phones on cameras, how that has completely changed the dynamic in our understanding of police behavior, especially against certain communities of color. And I will just tell you the difference in seeing the phone videos of what was going on in communities, when police for years had been saying, “Oh, they pulled a gun,” or, “They had drugs,” or this... And the people recording it could show exactly what happened and what went down, and that was so critically important to civil rights, to criminal justice reform, and making a huge impact. And again, that is what that tension is. What are you giving up? And you’re exactly right, the fear now is the supercharging. So, it’s not just one person’s phone. It’s like uploading all these videos, and then suddenly you have everyone being traced everywhere. The term is sousveillance, not surveillance. We’re all going to surveil each other and put it all on Facebook, and then AI can search Facebook and find us all. This exists today. What I’m getting at, very specifically, is the idea that you have no expectation of privacy in public might be changing culturally faster than it’s changing politically or legislatively. I’m curious if you see that balance changing state by state or at the federal level. This is the dynamic we’re in. We’re going to have little laboratories of democracy. It feels like Flock cameras are one little tick against “I have no expectation of privacy.” Actually, I want these gone. I don’t even want a license plate reader in my neighborhood because I want to feel that much less surveilled. And you could see a world where, as we understand how AI is impacting all of these abilities, we start to create certain spaces where you do have this expectation of privacy, and say, “Look, you cannot have cameras in public parks, or you can’t have cameras in blah, blah, blah.” It’s a really difficult balance, I think. When I think about it as a woman, just about certain areas... We’re just dealing with some of the college campuses and how to keep people safe there. And as I think about removing cameras from public spaces, I also think about the concerns we have about some of the attacks on women on college campuses. Again, I just keep getting to those tension points, and I think these are just things that we have to come together as a society and say that we’re willing to accept this amount of risk, or we’re not, or we’re going to have a cop on the beat to protect people, and we’re not going to have cameras, or we are in certain dark alleys. And that is the fear for me, though, is what you keep narrowing in on. It’s almost a little bit less about some of that, because all of that felt a little settled. It felt a little like, okay, we’re going to have some cameras out on some of these college campuses, and keep people safe. But adding that AI element takes it to a whole new, scarier level. And that’s why I think you’re saying we’re going to have to reopen these conversations. Well, you made a face when I said my Apple Watch was recording, or summarizing — I know, I can’t even have an Apple Watch because I can’t be looking at it every five minutes. So, I don’t do that- Do you think that Siri feature in the Apple Watch is appropriate, where it makes summaries of all your conversations? Again, where’s it going? Where are all these summaries going, and who’s looking at them, and why, and what are they doing with it? And are they uploading it into something? Is it anonymous? Is it not? Can they track it back to you? Who can hack into it? I mean, these are all the questions I have when I think about that. And that’s why I’m not wearing an Apple Watch. Fair enough. Apple has a lot of technical answers to your questions. I’m curious if they will ever come up with the social answers. I have one more question for you. It is a total wild card, but I’m dying to ask you. Oh. These are the ones that always get me. Okay, go. New Jersey is in the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, which, if enough states sign on, the presidency will be determined by the National Popular Vote winner. There are now enough new Democratic states with Democratic legislatures and Democratic governors that you could get it over the finish line. Are you going to push for that? I’m really excited about that. I hate the Electoral College. I’ve got to tell you, I love this idea. And I was seeing some of the same reporting that you were maybe looking into. So, this is something on my mind. One day I was going to take on the Electoral College. Today might be the day, so I got to get hot on this one and see where everybody’s at because I’d love to see a popular vote. Yeah. I’m rooting for it only because it would be a historic thing to happen in our lifetimes. But it does seem, from all of the headlines I saw after the election, I was like, oh, that is the most unlikely outcome. You really cannot be in the most densely populated state in the nation and not want to get rid of the Electoral College. That just doesn’t make any sense. I mean, if you just care about your vote and the power of your vote. Yeah. I think it’s a bunch of Midwest... I’m from the Midwest. There’s a bunch of Midwestern states that could sign on to it; we’ll do our best. If that happens, we’ll have you back. Actually, we should have you back to talk about privacy and all the things to come. Thank you so much, Governor Sherrill. This was great. I really appreciate it. Thanks for having me. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email! Decoder with Nilay Patel A podcast from The Verge about big ideas and other problems. SUBSCRIBE NOW!

articles.body:
President Trump is en route to Asia where he will meet with world leaders, including Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, this week.

He will first attend the ASEAN summit in the Philippines before heading to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit later in the week.

The national security controversy surrounding Nvidia looms large over Trump’s visit, as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faces scrutiny over his handling of AI chip export controls. Trump on Monday told reporters as he departed the White House that he “would not mind” Nvidia’s Jenson Huang being reinstated after the CEO resigned last week.

Back in Washington, the fight over who will lead Senate Democrats in the 120th Congress is also brewing. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) pushed back against a report from The Hill predicting Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) would win more than 40 votes in the Democratic leadership contest, calling it “a bunch of nonsense.

Meanwhile, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is looking to contain fallout from the weekend’s national groundstop blaming his predecessors and Congress for failing to adequately fund the nation’s aging air traffic control system.

Duffy also defended the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) decision to continue working with L3Harris, the telecommunications contractor blamed for the outage, saying the agency cannot simply cancel its contract.
