articles.title: Trump says it ‘certainly isn’t a bad idea’ for Jensen Huang to return to Nvidia
articles.summary: Trump told reporters he’s open to seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO, and commented on allegations Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy.
articles.body: Following Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO last week, Trump told reporters on Monday that he’s open to seeing Huang return and that he’s not certain that the woman Huang reportedly had an affair with was in fact a spy. “I think having Jensen go back– a lot of people are asking Jensen, they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea.” Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang return as CEO, adding, “I threw out the name of Tim Cook, but I would say that Jensen’s reinstatement– I think he learned a big lesson, I guess maybe one lesson more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that.” Trump has suggested Tim Cook step in as Nvidia’s CEO multiple times now. When asked about reports that Alice Huang, one of the women Jensen Huang allegedly had an affair with, was a Chinese spy, the president repeatedly claimed he wasn’t sure if it were true. “I don’t know that she’s a spy at all, nobody’s proven that,” Trump said. [Media: Trump also denied that Marco Rubio told him Alice Huang was a spy. “Usually what happens with that is that, any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy,” Trump said. “I don’t know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don’t. I don’t know that, you know, Jensen obviously has two things going. articles.title: Trump administration seeks to restrict China’s remote chip access after Nvidia scandal
articles.summary: The Trump administration is placing new restrictions on overseas data centers that provide China with remote access to computing power from advanced AI chips, after a high-profile spy scandal prompted new scrutiny of U.S. export restrictions. The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which manages export controls, announced a new rule Monday aiming to “ensure…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is placing new restrictions on overseas data centers that provide China with remote access to computing power from advanced AI chips, after a high-profile spy scandal prompted new scrutiny of U.S. export restrictions.

The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which manages export controls, announced a new rule Monday aiming to “ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements.”

The interim final rule, which takes effect in 90 days, will require a license for chips headed to overseas data centers that provide “significant” computing power to companies headquartered in restricted countries, like China.

It will also mandate a license for advanced chip exports to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, describing these as “countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.”

The move comes as the Commerce Department, which houses BIS, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are facing heat over their handling of chip export controls.

They came under scrutiny last week, after former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair, reportedly with a woman who U.S. officials concluded was working as a Chinese intelligence asset. He resigned as CEO early Thursday.

Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, put a spotlight on the Singapore-based data center company. The firm reportedly was under investigation by the Commerce Department over whether it helped smuggle Nvidia’s chips to China.

However, the probe was handed off to the Department of Justice last year, according to The New York Times.

The Times later reported that Lutnick has repeatedly clashed with top officials over how to regulate advanced technology and was seen as taking a softer line on Nvidia’s chip sales to China.

Lawmakers are now pushing for answers from both Lutnick and Jeffrey Kessler, head of BIS. Lutnick has agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee, while the House Foreign Affairs Committee has requested an appearance from Kessler.

articles.title: What to know about the Arkansas router that led to the FAA groundings
articles.summary: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) officials have indicated that a router at an Arkansas radio facility was one of two likely reasons behind the nationwide ground stop that temporarily grounded all U.S. flights last Friday. The agency stated on Sunday that preliminary findings point to the router in El Dorado, Ark., and a radar site in…
articles.body:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) officials have indicated that a router at an Arkansas radio facility was one of two likely reasons behind the nationwide ground stop that temporarily grounded all U.S. flights last Friday.

The agency stated on Sunday that preliminary findings point to the router in El Dorado, Ark., and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, both of which were viewed as reasons for the excessive data flooding the systems. Issues at both sites prompted the FAA to take them both offline, but a soaring rate of connections caused widespread failures, leading to the ground stop, The New York Times reported.

The national ground stop lasted for several hours on Friday and are still being felt days later. More than 10,000 flights within, into or out of the United States were delayed Sunday, and more than 2,300 were canceled, according to the flight-tracking website FlightAware . The incident marked the third nationwide ground stop, following a 90-minute outage in 2023 and on Sept. 11, 2001.

Here’s what to know about the router and what officials know likely led to the ground stop.

The FAA has sought to upgrade its copper-wire-based system with fiber optic cables. Employees were working to update the router at the El Dorado radio facility and had already upgraded the system weeks earlier, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday.

The FAA and L3Harris, the FAA’s current network service provider, had been working to upgrade the agency’s outdated technology before the ground stop. Duffy has said the expectation is to have all copper wires used by the FAA replaced by the end of 2028.

The issue was first noticed at the FAA’s Indianapolis, Ind., center, before more problems arose, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The FAA tasked employees with troubleshooting the problem before they located possible issues at the Arkansas and Texas sites. Both sites pinged the air traffic communications network before they were taken offline, disrupting other parts of the network, the FAA’s chief technology officer Rebecca Guy told reporters on Sunday.

Surge from the router spread to other facilities

“The FAA’s legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding the FAA [FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure] network, at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds,” the agency said Sunday. “This disrupted the system and created instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds.”

The surge also spread to backup routers at other radio facilities, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said Sunday, according to NBC News . The FAA then paused all flights to relieve the system, allowing officials to identify where the problem originated, which Bedford said was the “right call.”

Duffy told “This Week” host Martha Raddatz on ABC on Sunday that the router from Arkansas was in the “L3Harris lab down in Florida.” L3Harris was working at the El Dorado site to deploy a new router.

L3Harris said that in its work with the FAA, it “has completed more than 70 percent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system,” working to modernize the National Airspace System’s communications infrastructure.

“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” the company said in a statement . “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

The work to convert telecommunications at FAA facilities has been carried out at a rapid pace. FAA data states that more than 3,500 communication lines have been replaced, with more than 5,000 yet to be upgraded by 2028.

Duffy on Friday said the FAA needs Congress to provide $50 billion to overhaul the network, later saying that although funds allocated under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act have gone to the agency, Congress was “very specific in how we spend it.” He added that he does not “have money for … a new telecom system” or new software.

Former President Biden’s Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act provided the FAA with $5 billion, dolled out at about $1 billion per year over five years, toward the agency’s facilities and equipment. However, President Trump signed an executive order to pause disbursements from this law.

Trump accused Biden’s administration of making “an old and broken system” at the FAA “worse than when they began,” and called for Congress “to give the money, FAST!”

Trump’s law passed by Congress last year set aside $12.5 billion for the Department of Transportation to modernize its technology. But the issue of more funding has raised questions from some lawmakers, including Reps. Rick Larsen (D-Wash.) and Andre Carson (D-Ind.), who jointly said $11 billion of that money has not been spent.

“Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?” they said in a statement.

articles.title: Trump could’ve helped with falling prices ‘far earlier’: GasBuddy
articles.summary: As gas prices decrease across the country following months of soaring prices amid the Iran war, a leading petroleum analyst signaled President Trump could have helped lower fuel costs “far earlier.” The national average price for gasoline stood at $3.81 per gallon Monday, while diesel averaged just under $6 per gallon for the first time…
articles.body:
As gas prices decrease across the country following months of soaring prices amid the Iran war, a leading petroleum analyst signaled President Trump could have helped lower fuel costs “far earlier.”

The national average price for gasoline stood at $3.81 per gallon Monday, while diesel averaged just under $6 per gallon for the first time since September, according to AAA .

Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, argued that Americans could have felt some relief at the gas pump much sooner had Trump moved earlier to reduce tensions with Iran, where the deeply unpopular conflict disrupted global oil markets and drove up fuel costs.

“Had Trump chosen to make a deal with Iran or improve the geopolitical tensions earlier, gas prices would’ve declined earlier,” De Haan wrote Sunday on social platform X .

He was responding to a social media user who credited Trump for the recent decline in gas prices, pointing to the president’s prediction that the energy costs would fall after the midterm elections .

De Haan acknowledged that Trump’s signal earlier this month that he would not escalate the war after recent negotiations helped bring prices down, alongside state gas tax suspensions and seasonal trends. He noted the prolonged uncertainty surrounding the war had kept prices higher than necessary.

“[I]f the Iran situation had been resolved months and months ago prices would have fallen far earlier,” he wrote on X. “[B]y extending the uncertainty over Iran/Strait, high gas prices were extended.”

Gas prices reached a record high for an Election Day earlier this month, averaging $4.12 per gallon nationally, while diesel stood at $6.28 per gallon, according to GasBuddy data cited by De Haan.

Both Trump and Vice President Vance have said the Iran war played a role in Republicans’ crushing midterm defeats against Democrats, as the economic impact of the war on the American economy became a major faultline.

De Haan’s “ America’s Added Fuel Cost Clock ,” which estimates additional spending on gasoline and diesel since the conflict began, puts the total at roughly $159 billion compared with the same period last year. That includes nearly $96 billion in additional gasoline costs and more than $63 billion in diesel expenses.

articles.title: FBI says Artex AI open-source hacking tool used to breach networks in 'under three hours' | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The FBI says that the open-source hacking tool was used in cyberattacks targeting a U.S. IT giant and the South Korean financial industry.
articles.body:
The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry.

In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory , the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open-source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks.

Artex is one of several open-source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open-source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that makes it far more harder for human defenders to keep up.

In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.”

The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease.

Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information.

The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people.

The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers.

The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers.

A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to a request for comment about the FBI’s claim.

Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials.

“Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer Arve Kjoelen.

A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers.

After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open-source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks.

It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online , which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.

articles.title: US braces for loss of measles elimination status amid worst outbreak in decades
articles.summary: The U.S.’s measles elimination status is expected to be formalized this week, setting the stage for how the country will proceed in addressing the worst year for measles in more than three decades. For public health insiders, the U.S. losing its elimination status is already a foregone conclusion — it’s what authorities plan to do…
articles.body:
The U.S.’s measles elimination status is expected to be formalized this week, setting the stage for how the country will proceed in addressing the worst year for measles in more than three decades.

For public health insiders, the U.S. losing its elimination status is already a foregone conclusion — it’s what authorities plan to do in regaining it that concerns them now.

“Formally losing our elimination status is like a fire alarm going off. The emergency isn’t the alarm; it’s the fire,” Celine Gounder, an epidemiologist and editor-at-large for public health at KFF Health News, told The Hill.

The U.S. and Mexico met with the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) over the past week for a closed-door, three-day meeting to assess their respective measles elimination statuses. The U.S. achieved measles elimination in 2000, but the past two years have all but guaranteed this status to be lost.

Both countries met a key condition for losing their elimination statuses earlier this year: 12 continuous months of sustained domestic transmission. Canada has already lost its status and is engaged in a plan with PAHO to reverse this.

The number of confirmed measles cases this year has more than doubled last year’s — 5,412 this year as of Friday evening, compared with 2,289 in 2025 and just 285 in 2024. New York , Pennsylvania and Wisconsin have all reported measles-associated deaths , totaling 10 so far this year . For all three states, these were the first measles-related deaths they’d reported in more than three decades.

Citing anonymous sources, The Wall Street Journal reported Friday that PAHO revoked the U.S.’s status. An announcement from the organization is essentially just a formality at this point, confirming what experts have already acknowledged.

“My understanding is that this is a foregone conclusion that we’ve lost our elimination status, and it wasn’t just a matter of when the meeting was held to announce that determination, along with the country of Mexico losing its elimination status as well and joining dozens of countries that have been added to this list in the past year or two,” said David Margolius, director of the Cleveland Department of Public Health and chair-elect of the Big Cities Health Coalition.

The determination coming this week doesn’t seem likely to change how federal officials view the measles outbreak.

“Let’s say we did lose our measles elimination status. We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working ⁠with the states,” Erica Schwartz, director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said in an interview with Reuters.

Schwartz has faced criticism for her relative silence regarding the outbreak and for her agency’s exclusion of measles-related deaths reported by states from the national count.

While public health advocates have called for a stronger push from federal authorities, top officials such as Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and President Trump have clashed with state leaders over the outbreak, questioned whether deaths due to measles actually occurred and cast doubt on the efficacy of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine.

“The loss of our elimination status helps people outside of public health understand how dire the situation is. But public health leaders and elected officials should already have been responding,” Gounder said. “That Dr. Schwartz has done nothing to ramp up a measles vaccination response since taking office and still doesn’t plan to do so is damning.”

Gounder advised that the measles response should be tailored to meet the needs of different families who have not gotten vaccinated against measles, including those who haven’t because they lack access to healthcare and those who are ideologically opposed to immunization.

She also noted that schools play a significant role in how many young children get vaccinated.

“As a reminder, the school vaccination requirements are determined by the states, not by the CDC,” said Gounder. “In 2025 alone, you have nine states that made it easier to opt out of childhood vaccination requirements. Meanwhile, you have four states … that made it harder, that eliminated nonmedical exemptions, and that led to an increase in MMR vaccination rates of between 2 and 4 percentage points.”

The most recent data from the CDC found 92.4 percent of kindergartners in the 2025-2026 school year had received the MMR vaccine. The ideal coverage rate for preventing outbreaks is 95 percent, and the U.S. hasn’t met this level since before the COVID-19 pandemic.

At a more granular level, the national coverage rate includes counties where the vaccine coverage rate is extremely low, such as in southwestern Wisconsin, where coverage rates were as low as 42.3 percent last year.

Margolius said holding on to the same strategy taken by the federal government so far would be insufficient to counteract the measles outbreaks across the country, saying that the “messaging has to fundamentally change” and place emphasis on the “miracle of the public health innovation that we know vaccines to be.”

“There’s been no indication that it’s going to get better at this point, and so we would have to see a major change in the approach from the federal government at the very top, as well as this global cooperation that’s so essential,” he said.

Soon after the second Trump administration came into power, the U.S. withdrew from organizations such as the World Health Organization and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance . Both organizations play a significant role in global vaccination efforts and surveillance.

Margolius argued this rescinding of global support has ultimately backfired on the U.S., as higher international travel means outbreaks on the other side of the world can quickly become a problem domestically.

The Hill has reached out to HHS for comment on the expected announcement from PAHO.

articles.title: Freeze, fraud alert or monitoring? What to do after a breach
articles.summary: A credit freeze, fraud alert and identity monitoring each protect different parts of your financial life after a data breach. Here's how to choose.
articles.body: A data breach notice can leave you with plenty of questions. Should you freeze your credit? Is a fraud alert enough? Do you need an identity monitoring service? The right response depends on what information was exposed and whether someone has already tried to use it. Here's the important distinction. A company saying your information was involved in a breach does not automatically mean someone has opened an account in your name. An unfamiliar credit inquiry deserves attention, but it does not always prove fraud occurred. However, once you confirm someone has used your information fraudulently, the situation becomes more urgent. So, which protection should you choose? Let's look at what each one actually does. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. YOU HAVE A CREDIT FREEZE; IT STILL ISN’T ENOUGH What a credit freeze does A credit freeze restricts access to your credit file. It makes it harder for someone to open a new credit account in your name because most lenders need to review your credit information before approving an application. Credit freezes are completely free. You must place one separately with each of the three major credit bureaus: A freeze stays in place until you remove it, and it does not affect your credit score. If you apply for a mortgage, car loan or credit card, you may need to temporarily lift the freeze so the lender can review your report. You can do that for free. Employment and tenant-screening checks follow different rules and generally are not blocked by a credit freeze. A freeze is a strong option if your Social Security number was exposed or you simply want to reduce the risk of someone opening new credit in your name. However, it cannot protect an existing bank account, stop a scam payment or remove a fraudulent account that was already opened. What a fraud alert does A fraud alert tells lenders to take additional steps to verify your identity before approving new credit. Unlike a freeze, a fraud alert does not restrict access to your credit report. Instead, it warns lenders that someone may be trying to use your information. There are two main types: A fraud alert can be convenient if you're actively applying for a mortgage, loan or credit card and don't want to manage multiple credit freezes. Still, it offers less control than a freeze because lenders can continue accessing your credit file after completing the required identity checks. If someone has already opened an account fraudulently, placing an alert can help reduce additional risk. However, you'll still need to contact the creditor and dispute the fraudulent account. What identity monitoring does Identity monitoring watches for certain changes involving your personal or financial information and notifies you when suspicious activity appears. Depending on the service, those alerts may include: Monitoring is useful because it can give you an earlier warning that someone may be misusing your information. But there's an important limitation. Monitoring generally alerts you after suspicious activity is detected. It does not necessarily prevent that activity from happening. And no service can monitor everything. For example, basic credit monitoring may not detect an email account takeover, medical identity theft or a payment you authorized after being tricked by a scammer. Which tool fits your situation? The right protection depends on what happened to your information and whether someone has already tried to use it. Here's what to do in each situation. Your information was exposed, but you see no suspicious activity Start by reviewing the breach notice to understand exactly what information was involved. If passwords were exposed, change them immediately. Use unique passwords for each account and enable multifactor authentication, especially on your primary email account. If your Social Security number was compromised, consider freezing your credit with all three major bureaus right away. You can also take advantage of free credit monitoring offered by the affected company, if available. Just verify the offer through the company's official website. You notice an unfamiliar credit inquiry An unfamiliar credit inquiry deserves a closer look, but it doesn't always mean someone has stolen your identity. Contact the company listed on the inquiry using its official website or customer service number. Ask whether an application was submitted using your information. You should also review your credit reports from all three bureaus. You can get free weekly credit reports through AnnualCreditReport.com. If you suspect someone is trying to open credit in your name, consider placing a free credit freeze immediately while you investigate. You can also add a fraud alert. Someone opened an account in your name If you confirm that someone opened an account fraudulently, act immediately. Keep copies of your reports, correspondence and case numbers while the investigation continues. The problem involves your bank, phone or email account A credit freeze alone won't help if someone already has access to one of your existing accounts. Contact the financial institution or service provider immediately. If your bank account is involved, report unauthorized transactions and ask what protections can be placed on the account. If your email was compromised, change the password from a trusted device, review recovery information and sign out of unfamiliar sessions. And if your phone suddenly loses service for no obvious reason, contact your wireless carrier immediately. An unexpected loss of service can be a warning sign of a SIM-swap attack. WAS YOUR IDENTITY STOLEN? WHAT TO DO IN THE FIRST 24 HOURS What to do during the first week after a breach You don't need to spend the entire week worrying about what might happen. However, you should address the most serious risks right away. Also, watch out for follow-up scams. Criminals sometimes use major data breaches as an excuse to contact people with fake monitoring offers or recovery services. They may ask for your Social Security number, passwords or payment information. Don't trust a caller simply because they know details about the breach. Instead, verify offers by going directly to the affected company's official website. A simple decision guide Here's the easiest way to think about these protections. You can use more than one tool. In fact, a credit freeze and monitoring service can complement each other. Just remember that none of these options replaces contacting your bank, creditor or service provider when fraud has already occurred. When identity monitoring can complement a credit freeze A credit freeze makes it harder for criminals to open new credit accounts in your name, but it won't alert you to every suspicious change involving your personal information. An identity monitoring service can complement that protection by watching for certain warning signs. Depending on the plan, you may also have access to identity restoration specialists who can help you navigate disputes, documentation and recovery after identity theft. Neither tool guarantees complete protection, but together they can help you prevent certain problems and respond more quickly when suspicious activity appears. What to look for in an identity monitoring service Not all monitoring services offer the same protections. Before choosing one, consider these features: Keep in mind that identity monitoring cannot prevent every form of fraud or guarantee that suspicious activity will always be detected. You'll still need to contact your bank, credit card company or other affected institution directly if you discover unauthorized activity. The bottom line: A credit freeze can help prevent someone from opening new credit accounts, while identity monitoring can help you spot certain warning signs sooner. Using both can give you broader protection and make it easier to respond when something goes wrong. Pro tip: Keep your decision simple Ask one question first: am I trying to block new credit, receive an early warning or recover from confirmed fraud? A freeze focuses on blocking access, a fraud alert adds verification and monitoring provides visibility. You may use more than one, but you do not need to activate every tool simply because a breach occurred. 9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE Kurt's key takeaways One thing I've noticed about data breaches is that most people don't realize how vulnerable their personal information can be until something goes wrong. And by then, the damage may already be done. That's why I think it's smart to be proactive. A free credit freeze is a great place to start, but it only protects one part of your financial life. What I like about an identity protection service is that it adds another layer of protection by monitoring for suspicious activity that you might otherwise miss. And if someone does steal your identity, having access to restoration specialists can make a stressful situation easier to manage. No service can stop every scam, but having someone watching for warning signs and helping you respond can make a real difference. For me, it's about getting ahead of the problem rather than finding out about it after the damage is done. Have you ever discovered suspicious activity involving your personal information, and would an identity monitoring service give you greater peace of mind? articles.title: OpenAI unveils tool to better detect child sexual abuse material
articles.summary: OpenAI released a new tool Monday aimed at detecting possible child sexual abuse material (CSAM), including content made with artificial intelligence. The image classifier, which will be available for vetted organizations and law enforcement investigators focused on online safety, was trained and tested to identify visual signs of abuse. The company said it is the…
articles.body:
OpenAI released a new tool Monday aimed at detecting possible child sexual abuse material (CSAM), including content made with artificial intelligence.

The image classifier , which will be available for vetted organizations and law enforcement investigators focused on online safety, was trained and tested to identify visual signs of abuse. The company said it is the first image classifier with a “specific signal” for AI-generated content that may contain CSAM.

Its release comes as AI companies, much like social media companies the past decade, face mounting pressure to help curb CSAM from being spread or made on their platforms.

Comparing the classifier to current tools, OpenAI said its new product was better at not flagging false positives, flagging about 48 percent fewer images while still finding about the same number of abusive images as existing tools.

The AI firm’s tool also flagged images about twice as likely to contain abuse, according to the ChatGPT maker.

The classifier will still require human review to ensure accuracy, company leaders said Monday. It was made with the help of the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, the Tech Coalition and ROOST (the Robust Online Safety Tools) project.

OpenAI’s models already ban CSAM and are trained to refuse requests to generate it. The company announced Monday they are introducing a new product warning in ChatGPT that appears during attempts to find the explicit material and direct users to behavioral resources.

“The warning makes clear that sexualizing children causes harm, including when the requested material is AI-generated,” the company said in a blog post. “Alongside the warning, we’ll remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours, while keeping specialist support available to help people stop harmful behavior.”

The firm continued, “Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions and ultimately account closure or reports to authorities.”

John Buckley, OpenAI’s head of child safety public policy, said the company’s teams heard of capacity issues from law enforcement during the development of this product.

“We want to make sure that our tooling is available to support them to do a really effective job at triaging, getting to high-risk cases much more quickly,’ Buckley told reporters Monday.

“Our tool needs to be at the hands of organizations who can deal with CSAM, we do not want to hand this tool out individual developers who are not equipped with the specialized review that’s required or registered to report to NMEC or other international reporting hotlines,” he added.

articles.title: OpenAI wants to stop deepfakes from overwhelming child abuse tiplines
articles.summary: OpenAI introduced a new classifier to detect AI-generated child sexual abuse material that it says can cut down on human reviewer workload.
articles.body: OpenAI is announcing a tool that it says will help child sexual abuse investigators cut through the noise to find harmful material they can act on quickly. At a Monday press briefing in Washington, DC, OpenAI announced a classifier it says can better detect abusive imagery of kids, including whether it’s AI-generated. It’s also offering free access to vetted organizations, giving developers more guidance on how to detect this type of content, and helping to train law enforcement on how AI can aid their investigations. The news comes as policymakers and others are pushing for more safety restrictions on AI tools, accusing OpenAI and other companies of facilitating harm to children. In recent years, AI-generated sexual images of children have threatened to overwhelm systems like the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) CyberTipline, which collects and triages reports of child sexual abuse material (CSAM). The CyberTipline received 400,000 generative AI-related reports in 2025, an exponential increase from the 67,000 it received in 2024, and researchers have warned that the influx could make NCMEC’s workload “unmanageable.” The US government has stated that both AI-generated and non-AI-generated CSAM is illegal, and 48 states have laws to address sexually explicit AI deepfakes. But the tools to make them are widely available, and researchers say that a flood of fake images can make it harder to tell when a child is actively experiencing harm. North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson, who cochairs the AG Alliance’s AI Task Force, said at OpenAI’s event that the influx of AI-generated CSAM reports to NCMEC is “explosive” — and if they keep going that way, “it is going to mean that we fail in our mission.” Tech companies are facing a range of policy proposals that could require them to take more action against CSAM and other potentially harmful content for kids. The Take It Down Act now requires social media platforms to remove real or AI-generated nonconsensual intimate images within 48 hours, and the newly elected Congress could seek to take stronger action against AI companies like SpaceXSI, whose Grok chatbot went on an undressing spree earlier this year. Last month eight states sued OpenAI for a separate set of alleged harms to children, citing lawsuits alleging ChatGPT encouraged illegal substance use and suicide. OpenAI says its classifier dramatically cuts down on false positives, flagging 48 percent fewer images, while the images it did identify were twice as likely to contain abusive material. It’s designed to catch abusive AI-generated images produced by a variety of tools, including open-source models and nudifying apps. It’s also the first broadly available CSAM classifier with a specific flag for AI-generated material, said OpenAI’s head of child safety public policy, John Buckley, at the briefing. “It’s important for industry to be able to understand what images may contain a fictional child versus a real child,” Buckley added. “That triage is critical in law enforcement reporting flows.” He also emphasized, however, that laws should recognize the harm of AI-generated CSAM: “It potentially erodes social norms in offending against children, and it’s often found colocated with child sexual abuse imagery of real children,” Buckley said. OpenAI’s own ChatGPT image generator is designed to deny user requests for CSAM. Now, users who attempt to produce it will be shown a new warning developed with expert guidance to try to encourage them to seek help. A first offense will trigger a 24-hour pause in accessing ChatGPT and warn the user their account could be permanently closed, while offering support resources to combat the behavior. OpenAI says it reports “all instances of CSAM” to NCMEC. In a statement, Buckley explained that the 24-hour pause is based on expert advice for best practices “and international evidence on what works to prevent and respond to CSAM seeking vs CSAM generation.” The point is “to interrupt harmful behavior and direct people toward specialist help to stop it.” Jackson said that North Carolina and many other states now have laws that cover synthetic CSAM, but that partnering with a tech company like OpenAI to help deter its creation is a fairly novel approach to an emerging issue. “Most of what AGs do is accountability work,” he told reporters at the briefing. “Most of our jurisdiction kicks in after the fact to hold people accountable for harm. But with this, we wanted to see if it was possible to develop a model of working together to prevent that harm. And I would say it’s still basically an experiment.”

articles.title: Airfare, gas prices expected to impact Thanksgiving travel: AAA
articles.summary: Americans concerned over higher fuel costs this year are likely to see gas prices and airfare prices have an impact on travel over the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday, according to AAA. The travel agency announced Monday that it projects 81.5 million American will travel at least 50 miles from home between Nov. 24-30. This prediction is…
articles.body:
Americans concerned over higher fuel costs this year are likely to see gas prices and airfare prices have an impact on travel over the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday, according to AAA.

The travel agency announced Monday that it projects 81.5 million American will travel at least 50 miles from home between Nov. 24-30. This prediction is lower than 2025’s outcome of 81.6 million people who traveled for Thanksgiving, at around 121,000 fewer travelers, and ends the three-year streak of record-high travel for the November holiday.

Of that projection, 72.9 million people are expected to travel by car, down from 73.1 million last year. AAA said this was due to steeper prices at the pump after record highs in August, September and October.

The national average price of gasoline has never ticked over $4 per gallon on Thanksgiving Day. The last time prices were high during the holiday was in 2022, when it reached $3.58.

That average has decreased in recent weeks after reaching $4 per gallon earlier this year in the months after the start of the Iran war. The average as of Monday reached $3.81.

AAA also projects that 5.96 million travelers will take domestic flights for the holiday, a decrease by 0.2 percent over last year. The association attributed this to the cost of travel, with roundtrip domestic flights having increased by 17 percent at an average of $800 per ticket. The travel agency urged that people consider secondary airports further from home that “could deliver meaningful savings.”

Other forms of travels — such as public transportation or cruises — will see a 4.1 percent increase from last year, with 2.6 million Americans taking alternate forms of transportation.

“After three years of record highs, the number of travelers is slightly lower partly because of higher travel costs this year,” AAA Travel Vice President Stacey Barber said in a statement. “But travelers won’t notice much of a difference on the roads and at the airports, since projected volumes remain near record levels.”

The cost of gas has been a key issue for many Americans who commute or travel, becoming enough of a factor in the 2026 midterm elections that Democratic and Republican candidates called for an end to the conflict with Iran to lower gas prices.

The Trump administration responded to this concern, tapping into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and making a deal with Russia to receive diesel amid skyrocketing prices, among other solutions.

Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said Trump could have helped lower fuel costs much sooner. The longer-than-predicted conflict with Iran and its shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz “extended” those high prices, he said.

“Had Trump chosen to make a deal with Iran or improve the geopolitical tensions earlier, gas prices would’ve declined earlier,” De Haan wrote Sunday on social platform X .

articles.title: Uber says hackers stole information on close to 150,000 driver's licenses during data breach | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The ride-sharing giant said driver's license information stored by AI cloud company Fireworks AI was stolen during a security incident.
articles.body:
Uber is notifying close to 150,000 drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers.

In notices filed this week with several U.S. attorneys general, including California and Iowa , the ride-hailing giant said it was notified on October 9 by the provider that hackers broke in and stole internal credentials, which were used to access Uber’s data.

The company said it subsequently began notifying affected drivers that their personal information was stored with the provider.

The stolen data includes affected drivers’ names, addresses, dates of birth, and driver’s license numbers.

TechCrunch has learned that the provider is Fireworks AI, which lets developers access and use open-weight AI models. Fireworks reported a data breach last month in which hackers stole its customers’ information, including billing data and some private AI datasets.

Online productivity startup Notion and AI coding startup Cursor have both confirmed that they had data stolen during the Fireworks hack.

In Uber’s case, the company said it had alerts enabled to detect unauthorized access to its Fireworks environment, but because the hackers used Fireworks’ own internal credentials, “no alerts were triggered.”

When reached for comment, an Uber spokesperson told TechCrunch: “The notices to drivers are in relation to a security incident impacting one of our third-party vendors, Fireworks.ai, which had access to some Uber data,” and deferred our questions to Fireworks.

A spokesperson for Fireworks confirmed that the company identified a security issue involving unauthorized access to some of its systems, which affected customer data, but the spokesperson did not address our questions about the incident.

Fireworks attributed its breach to a financially motivated cybercriminal group whose goals are to sell stolen tokens for accessing large language models, or LLMs. No known cybercriminal group has taken credit for the data theft.

In a notice filed with Oregon’s attorney general, Uber said it notified 149,346 people in total that their information had been taken in the breach at Fireworks.

TechCrunch previously reported that Uber has notified drivers in California, Illinois, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and South Carolina. We’ve also seen data breach notices filed in Texas and Vermont.

When asked by TechCrunch, Uber’s spokesperson did not say how many drivers are affected by the breach, nor how many drivers it was notifying about the incident.

It’s unclear if the number of affected drivers is expected to rise, and Uber did not respond to a follow-up email sent Monday.

This is Uber’s second known data breach this year. The company reported a security incident at its Uber Freight truck shipping unit, for which an extortion gang took credit for stealing data.

First published on November 13, and updated with a response from Fireworks, and again with a new updated figure of affected individuals from Oregon’s attorney general.

articles.title: America hits a tech wall as outages cripple email, ground flights and disrupt major banks
articles.summary: A wave of tech failures hit Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo online banking Monday, days after a Microsoft 365 outage and FAA ground stop.
articles.body: America’s digital lifelines are hitting a rough patch, with a string of technology failures disrupting inboxes, grounding flights and delaying bank transactions in just five days. The latest trouble surfaced Monday as customers at major banks, including Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo, reported problems accessing online services. Chase later confirmed to Fox News that transactions were processing normally, while Bank of America said its systems had operated normally throughout the day. "Transactions are processing normally," JPMorgan Chase spokesperson told Fox News Digital Monday evening. PERPETUAL PARALYSIS: WHY EVERYTHING IS GRINDING TO A HALT Chase had earlier said a technical issue was slowing some transactions but customers still had access to their accounts and funds. A source familiar with the Chase outage told Fox News the problem was a technical bug, not a cyber issue. Wells Fargo acknowledged the outage on its website, saying online banking wasn't available Monday afternoon. "We're having technical issues, but we’re working to resolve them as quickly as possible," a message on Wells Fargo's website said. "Please try again later." The banking problems followed disruptions at Microsoft and human resources software provider Workday, along with a nationwide FAA ground stop that upended air travel. 4 CRITICAL TRAVEL ISSUES FOR THOSE DELAYED AND DISRUPTED BY FAA NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP Here is a timeline of the technology turmoil: Nov. 12: Microsoft outage disrupts email worldwide A widespread Microsoft 365 outage disrupted Outlook, Teams and other services, leaving users struggling to access email and other functions. The incident began Thursday and lasted nearly 24 hours, with service restored Friday morning, according to Microsoft’s preliminary incident report. Email suffered the most significant disruption, while the impact on other services varied. Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna attributed the failure to a combination of a previously undetected software defect, increased traffic and reduced server capacity. Microsoft says more than 430 million people use its Microsoft 365 apps. That figure represents the platform’s user base, rather than a confirmed tally of people affected. Nov. 13: FAA ground stop brings departures to a halt The FAA halted departures nationwide for nearly five hours Friday after technical problems destabilized aircraft communications and radar feeds. The disruption began around 3:30 p.m. Eastern, with air traffic resuming at 8:15 p.m., according to the agency. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the problems began when contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. was replacing old copper wiring with fiber wiring in the air traffic control system, causing a system overload. BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS The work led to intermittent communications and radar gaps. Duffy said officials were investigating whether contractor incompetence or a faulty router was responsible. "Our contractor didn’t meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment," Duffy said. NBA AND NHL TEAMS BATTLE DELAYS AS NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP DISRUPTS WEEKEND SPORTS TRAVEL Some radio frequencies and radar feeds remained operational, and every aircraft landed safely, according to the FAA. Operators canceled approximately 12,462 flights Friday, including 9,082 by major airlines, the FAA said, while cautioning that not all cancellations were directly caused by the ground stop. UPDATED START TIMES FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL GAMES AFFECTED BY FAA GROUND STOP, BROKEN DOWN BY CONFERENCE The agency said it had no indication of a cyberattack. Nov. 13: Workday outage locks employees out Workday, whose payroll and human resources software is used by millions of employees, experienced a widespread outage Friday, a day after Microsoft’s disruption. The platform manages services for about 11,500 companies, including Walmart, Target, Netflix, Southwest Airlines and PNC Bank. Its clients also include government agencies and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, though not all customers reported outages. "Workday is currently unavailable," a message shown to users said. "We are experiencing a service interruption. Your service will be restored as quickly as possible." Outage-tracking website Downdetector recorded a spike of nearly 3,000 reports shortly after 5 p.m. Friday. "Some of our customers are experiencing a service disruption, and we’re working urgently to investigate and resolve the issue," a Workday spokesperson told Fox News. "We sincerely apologize for the challenges this is causing impacted customers." Nov. 16: Major bank customers report online problems Customers at Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo reported online banking difficulties Monday, adding banking to the list of everyday services hit by technology trouble. Chase initially said some transactions were taking longer than usual but customers retained access to their accounts and money. The bank later confirmed to Fox News that transactions were processing normally. The incident was traced to a software release JPMorgan Chase rolled out earlier Monday that affected a subset of its systems. There was no indication of malicious or external cyber activity. The impact was limited to JPMorgan Chase and transactions at other financial institutions in which JPMorgan Chase was a party. JPMorgan Chase initially said systems were coming back online and the incident was not malicious. "Bank of America systems have been operating normally today. Clients experiencing delays with other providers may wish to contact them directly for the latest information," Bank of America said in a statement. The extent and causes of the reported problems at the other banks were not immediately clear. Zelle told FOX Business its payment network was operating normally, but problems at financial institutions could be delaying payments for some customers. "Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds." "An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers. Please contact them directly," Zelle added. Fox News' CB Cotton and Robert McGreevy contributed to this report.

articles.title: US data centers emit more greenhouse gases than Denmark, Harvard study finds
articles.summary: A new study conducted by researchers at Harvard found the top 400 U.S. data centers emitted more greenhouse gases last year than Denmark. The study looked at 403 hyper-scaled data centers across the U.S. to estimate annual electricity consumption for each facility between May 2024 and April 2025 under certain scenarios. It found the facilities —…
articles.body:
A new study conducted by researchers at Harvard found the top 400 U.S. data centers emitted more greenhouse gases last year than Denmark.

The study looked at 403 hyper-scaled data centers across the U.S. to estimate annual electricity consumption for each facility between May 2024 and April 2025 under certain scenarios. It found the facilities — depending on how hard they were running — used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours of electricity.

Within the time period, data center electricity demand accounted for an estimated 1.8 percent of total U.S. electricity consumption and 25.7 million metric tons of CO2. Researchers noted the estimate was two to three times higher than an estimate from 2018.

The study observed that 54 percent of electricity that supports data centers was from fossil fuels, of which 30 percent was natural gas and 15 percent was coal.

One of the major takeaways researchers pointed out was the location of the data centers, as “many of the facilities were concentrated in geographic areas where electricity is generated heavily by coal-fired power plants.”

Researchers also reported that 4 states accounted for more than half of the electricity use analyzed: Virginia, Ohio, Oregon and Iowa.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” lead author Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral fellow at Harvard, wrote in a press release .

“The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025,” he said. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”

Data centers have caused bipartisan backlash as Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) called on the Senate to pass a data center construction moratorium on Nov. 11, while his Democratic colleagues have demanded developer accountability.

Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) push ed legislation aiming to speed the buildout of data center infrastructure but would require developers to pay more for their electricity use. They hope to vote on it during the upper chamber’s lame-duck session in November.

articles.title: Nvidia’s board not considering return of Huang as CEO
articles.summary: Nvidia’s Board of Directors is not weighing Jensen Huang’s return as CEO, a source familiar confirmed to The Hill. Within days of Huang stepping down as Nvidia’s longtime CEO amid a national security scandal, petitions circulated calling for his return, while President Trump said on Monday he “certainly wouldn’t mind” if Huang returned as CEO.…
articles.body:
Nvidia’s Board of Directors is not weighing Jensen Huang’s return as CEO , a source familiar confirmed to The Hill.

Within days of Huang stepping down as Nvidia’s longtime CEO amid a national security scandal, petitions circulated calling for his return, while President Trump said on Monday he “certainly wouldn’t mind” if Huang returned as CEO.

Huang resigned last Thursday, days after admitting he had an extramarital affair. Reports indicated it was with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials believe may be a Chinese spy, the New York Times reported.

The former CEO has not yet made his own statement, yet the Financial Times reported he is discussing a comeback with allies in Silicon Valley. Several tech exectuives signed an open letter calling for his reinstatement, including SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.

The executives argued Huang should be brought back while an independent investigation is completed. Nvidia’s board started an investigation last week before Huang resigned, while lawmakers on Capitol Hill are launching probes of their own.

The open letter, which has more than 170,000 signatories, asked the board to “provide compelling evidence that [Huang’s] removal is in Nvidia’s best interests,” and stated the former CEO “deserves due process, not mob justice.”

When asked if he would like to see Huang reinstated, Trump responded, “I would not mind. I would not mind that.”

“I think he learned a big lesson,” he continued. “I guess maybe one lesson more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that.”

Trump again floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook as a replacement for Huang at Nvidia.

Trump declined to say whether he thinks Huang is a spy, stating, “I don’t know that she’s a Chinese spy, and I’ve said that. I don’t know that she’s a Chinese spy. We’ll determine that.”

The president is on his way to Asia, where he will meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping. AI, trade and security issues are expected to be top agenda discussion items.

Customers at Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Truist are reporting trouble accessing their accounts following Microsoft Outlook’s major outage last week.

A J.P. Morgan-Chase Bank spokesperson told The Hill its systems were experiencing “a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems,” adding “there is no evidence this is cyber-related.”

“It is taking longer than usual to service some customers,” the spokesperson continued. “This is not a systemic issue – other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.”

The bank stated customers would still be able to access their accounts and funds as Chase works to resolve the issue by “the end of the day today.”

Another spokesperson from U.S. Bank told The Hill in a statement that its systems “are not directly impacted” but “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”

Outage tracker website Downdector reports that customers of Chase, Bank of America, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo are most heavily affected. Of the reports made by Chase customers, 52 percent were concerned account balances and transactions, 21 percent with web log-ins and 17 percent with transfers and wires.

When attempting to access the Chase mobile app, customers are met with messages reading, “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”

For U.S. Bank customers, 29 percent reported issues with online banking, 27 percent with the mobile app and 23 percent with transferring funds. At Wells Fargo, 44 percent reported issues with account balances and transactions, 31 percent with logging into their accounts and 15 percent with about Zelle-related transactions.

Zelle reportedly told NewsNation , The Hill’s partner, its services are not down and are “operating as it should.”

“Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds,” the company stated, per NewsNation. “An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers. Please contact them directly.”

This comes after a nationwide outage was reported Thursday for Microsoft’s Outlook and Teams, interrupting work for companies, as well as congressional offices and city governments. At one sheriff’s office in Colorado, the Outlook outage affected its online bond payment platform for people being held in their detention facility.

articles.title: Apple reveals new Mac security controls as AI agents raise privacy risks | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Following an October announcement, Apple has detailed new permission controls, warnings, and transparency features coming to macOS 27.3 to address risks posed by AI agents and other apps.
articles.body:
As promised last month , Apple on Monday announced changes to Mac security controls designed to protect users’ data from the growing popularity of AI agents and their apps’ demand for “full disk access.”

“Before granting an app such extraordinary access, users should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk,” Apple warned in its blog post aimed at app developers.

Unlike AI chatbots that simply answer questions, agents run on a user’s device where they can take actions across the operating system, files, and apps on the user’s behalf.

While the tools can be useful, Apple has grown concerned about the increased risks to users’ data and privacy that these AI agents introduce. At the same time, the company has been benefiting from sales of Mac minis and Mac Studio computers that AI early adopters have been purchasing specifically to run their local AI models.

To balance these competing interests, Apple said in October that it would revise some of its security settings around Mac apps. The announcement followed two notable incidents involving AI agents. In one, a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app read their private messages without consent; a separate report from Wired cited a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app that could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data.

Now, Apple is sharing the changes it’s making.

For starters, it’s splitting up Device Control and Data Access into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. The changes are designed to help users better understand that selecting the first option means overriding built-in security protections.

To streamline configurations, Apple says there will now also be a single method for granting permissions that involves selecting the requested app from a list. The company will also introduce new guidance encouraging users to grant access only to the specific apps that need it when they enable the System & App Protection Override setting. Similar guidance will appear when users enable Full Disk Access to allow an app to access their folders.

The company will also provide users with “increased visibility into the wide range of data apps will receive access to or control over if full permissions are granted,” the blog post notes.

Another change will give users more granular control over when an AI agent or app can gain access by allowing users to configure their apps to ask for permission every time access is needed. While arguably tedious and a potential obstacle to true automation, the feature could allow users to experiment with local AI without giving the agent carte blanche.

There will also be a new transparency indicator that appears when an app is controlling another app through the System & App Protection Override option.

The changes, which are arriving with macOS 27.3, don’t appear to prevent Mac users from installing and running AI agents or other apps that ask for higher levels of access. Instead, they give users more nuanced options, control, and information about the choices they’re making.

Apple advises app developers to adjust their onboarding processes to account for the new changes and suggests that their apps learn to “gracefully handle having access to only a limited set of folders or apps.”

Developers of apps that request Full Disk Access for disk backup or to provide assistive technologies can request exceptions to the new rules (which Apple calls “entitlements”) to preserve the same functionality they offered before the macOS 27.3 update.

articles.title: Fake E-ZPass email threatens $100 fine over unpaid toll
articles.summary: A fake E-ZPass email cites a real federal regulation to demand toll payments, but the law it references has nothing to do with collecting tolls.
articles.body: You open your email and see a warning from E-ZPass. Apparently, there's a problem with your toll account, and a payment didn't go through. Maybe you recently drove through a toll plaza. Maybe your credit card expired. Either way, it's the kind of message that makes you wonder whether you owe money. And that's exactly what scammers are counting on. We recently received a convincing fake E-ZPass email claiming an overdue toll could trigger additional penalties and even affect your vehicle's registration renewal. The message includes familiar E-ZPass branding and an official-looking violation number. There's even a big purple "Pay Now" button. But take a closer look, and several warning signs point to a phishing scam. And here's what I find especially interesting. The scammers behind this email even borrowed language from federal regulations to make their payment demands sound legitimate. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. FAKE AAA EMAIL SCAM TARGETS DRIVERS How this fake E-ZPass email scam works The email arrived with a subject line reading "Your E-ZPass Account Has an Overdue Balance." The sender identified itself as "E-ZPass Violations Dept #276797." The message displayed the E-ZPass logo and included a violation reference number. It even listed Nov. 6 as the issue date. The headline gets straight to the point: "Your toll payment could not be processed." According to the message, a recent toll crossing could not be charged because of insufficient funds, a declined credit card or an expired payment method. That explanation sounds believable because payment problems can happen with legitimate toll accounts. Then comes the pressure. The email warns that unpaid balances could be referred to collections. It also threatens a civil penalty of up to $100 per violation and a possible hold on vehicle registration renewal. To make those claims sound official, the message cites a federal regulation. Below the warning, the recipient sees a large "Pay Now" button. There are also options to update a payment method or dispute the alleged violation. The apparent goal is to scare someone into following a link that could lead to a fraudulent payment website. From there, scammers may try to steal credit card information or other sensitive details. Warning signs that reveal the fake E-ZPass email At first, this email looks like a legitimate toll notice. But once you start looking at the details more closely, several red flags suggest something is wrong. Here's what caught our attention. The sender's email address looks suspicious One of the biggest clues appears in the email details. Although the message claims to come from E-ZPass, the actual sender address ends in @cashcoma.cooljz.com. The reply-to address also uses that unrelated domain. That's a major warning sign. Scammers can make the sender's display name say almost anything. They can also copy official logos to make their messages look convincing. However, the underlying email address can reveal something very different. In this example, the recipient field also displays noreply@ezpassviolations.com. That might look official, but an address appearing in the "To" field says nothing about who actually sent the email. Even when an address looks familiar, it's worth checking. Criminals can spoof sender information to impersonate legitimate organizations. The email tells you to move it out of spam At the top of the message, a notice says that if the email lands in your junk or spam folder, you should move it to your inbox. It also asks you to add the sender to your safe sender list. So, an email demanding payment is also asking you to override your email provider's spam warning. Legitimate senders sometimes ask people to check their spam folders. However, in this case, the request appears alongside suspicious sender information and a threatening payment notice. The email had already landed in the junk folder. That alone doesn't prove fraud, but it gives you another reason to investigate before clicking anything. The federal regulation doesn't support the payment demand This may be the most revealing detail in the entire email. The message references 23 CFR Part 940, suggesting federal regulations require drivers to settle outstanding toll balances under the conditions described in the notice. There's a big problem with that claim. 23 CFR Part 940 covers intelligent transportation system architecture and standards. It addresses how certain transportation technology systems are developed and implemented. It does not establish the blanket toll payment obligation suggested by this email. The reference to federal law gives the warning an appearance of authority, even though the cited regulation doesn't support the payment demand. And let's be realistic: how many of us would stop to look up a federal regulation while worrying about an overdue bill? That's what makes this tactic so concerning. FAKE SOCIAL SECURITY STATEMENT EMAIL HIDES A SCAM The $100 penalty creates unnecessary panic The email warns that you could face a $100 civil penalty, additional fees and even trouble renewing your vehicle's registration. That's enough to make anyone nervous, especially when the email doesn't even tell you how much you supposedly owe in tolls. And here's something else that caught my attention. There's no toll crossing location, no license plate number and no date showing when the alleged violation happened. The email does include a violation reference number, but don't let that fool you. Scammers can easily make up a string of letters and numbers to make a message look official. Now, real toll violations can come with penalties, depending on the toll agency and its rules. But if an unexpected email suddenly threatens you with fines or registration problems, you should verify the claim directly with your toll agency before taking any action. Why fake E-ZPass scams keep targeting drivers For years, many toll phishing scams arrived as text messages. Drivers would receive a warning about an unpaid balance, followed by a link demanding immediate payment. We previously reported on fake toll road texts targeting drivers across America. Those schemes directed victims to fraudulent payment websites designed to collect financial information. The email we reviewed uses a similar approach, but its polished appearance gives scammers another way to reach potential victims. The E-ZPass Group has warned about fraudulent emails and text messages impersonating toll agencies. It also explains that the E-ZPass Group itself does not hold customer accounts or collect toll payments. Individual member agencies handle those services. The problem has become significant enough to show up in federal fraud data. In May, the Federal Trade Commission reported that government imposter scam reports rose 40% in 2025. The agency said bogus overdue toll notices contributed to that increase. Those messages often threaten additional fees or registration problems if drivers fail to pay quickly. It's a familiar tactic, but scammers continue to find ways to make their warnings more convincing. We reached out to the E-ZPass Group for comment on this particular email and to ask whether it has seen similar messages targeting drivers, but did not receive a response before our deadline. How to protect yourself from fake E-ZPass emails A suspicious toll notice can catch you off guard, especially when it threatens fines or registration problems. Before you click anything or make a payment, here are a few simple steps I recommend taking to protect yourself. 1. Check your E-ZPass account directly Open the official website or app for your toll provider. Avoid using the payment button inside a suspicious email. Instead, sign in through the website you normally use. Look for outstanding balances or payment problems there. If you have questions, contact your toll agency using its published customer service number. For example, New York E-ZPass customers can visit E-ZPass New York at e-zpassny.com/. Other states and toll agencies operate their own official websites. If the email claims you have a violation, ask the agency to verify it using your account information. 2. Never trust an unexpected payment link Avoid clicking "Pay Now" or "Update Payment Method" in an email you cannot verify. A fraudulent payment page may look almost identical to the real website. Once you enter your credit card information, scammers could use it to make unauthorized charges. For more ways to recognize suspicious links, see our CyberGuy article on how to spot and prevent phishing attacks in your inbox. 3. Look closely at the sender's address Check the complete sender and reply-to addresses. Don't rely on the displayed name or logo. If you see unfamiliar domains or addresses that don't match the organization, treat the message as suspicious. Keep in mind that even a familiar-looking sender address can be spoofed. That's why independently verifying an unexpected payment request remains so important. 4. Don't let threats rush you into paying Take time to verify any warning about fines or registration problems. Scammers often use threats because fear can make people act without thinking. An alarming message deserves additional scrutiny, especially when it references legal consequences without providing enough information to verify the alleged violation. IS THAT TRAFFIC TICKET TEXT A SCAM OR REAL? 5. Use strong antivirus protection Keep strong antivirus software installed and updated on your devices. Security software can help detect malicious websites and potentially harmful downloads. Some products also offer phishing protection that warns you when a link leads to a suspicious website. However, antivirus protection cannot guarantee that every fake payment page will be blocked. You still need to verify unexpected requests before sharing information. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 6. Report the suspicious email Report the message as phishing through your email provider. You can also file a complaint with the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov or the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/. Include the suspicious sender address and details about the message. If possible, preserve the email until you've submitted your report. After reporting it, delete the message. 7. Consider using a data removal service Reduce the personal information scammers can find about you online. Data brokers collect and sell information such as your name, address and phone number. Criminals can potentially use those details to make phishing messages more convincing. A data removal service can help remove your information from participating data broker websites, making it harder for scammers to find. While it won't stop every fake E-ZPass email, it can help reduce your exposure to targeted scams. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. What to do if you already clicked or paid Accidentally clicked a link in a suspicious E-ZPass email? Don't panic. The next steps depend on what happened after you opened it. Here's how to protect yourself and limit any potential damage. Kurt's key takeaways What really caught my attention about this scam was the reference to federal regulations. That's pretty clever on the scammers' part because most of us aren't going to look up a law when we're worried about an overdue bill. And the email looks polished enough that someone could easily overlook the strange sender address. I can see how someone might fall for it, especially if they've recently driven through a toll. My advice is to never pay an unexpected bill through a link in an email. Go directly to the toll agency and check your account. That extra step could save you a lot of trouble. Have you ever received a toll violation notice that looked so convincing you almost paid it? Or have scammers actually managed to get your money? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.
