articles.title: Marc Andreessen says government regulation will save jobs from AI — at the cost of economic growth
articles.summary: The venture capitalist says job losses in government-regulated sectors will be insulated from major job losses, but those regulations will limit economic and...
articles.body:
Venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, co-head of Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh's task force on jobs and productivity, predicted that artificial intelligence will have a dual effect in the job market: Job losses in government-regulated sectors will be insulated from major job losses, but those regulations will limit economic and productivity growth.

"You might interpret this as good news because it means a revolution is not going to destroy all the jobs or kill everybody," he said. "You could also view this as very negative, which is productivity growth just simply may not grow very much. Economic growth just simply may not grow very much."

Andreessen sees two categories of economic sectors: fast-moving sectors that see rapid technological and economic change, along with rapid job turnover — industries like consumer electronics and media entertainment. The other sectors are a combination of law and government, which are not structured to change rapidly and are typically characterized by extensive subsidization.

That means the fastest-growing sectors will see their prices go down, while the slower-growing regulated or government-subsidized sectors will see their prices go up.

"Your iPhone's getting cheaper, the flat-screen TV on your wall is getting cheaper. The bad news is college education is going to cost a million bucks, healthcare is becoming unaffordable, and good luck buying a house," he said.

Follow Jennifer Schonberger on X @Jenniferisms and on Instagram .

articles.title: Cyber giant Infoblox confirms security incident after hackers access 'company information' | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The cybersecurity and automation giant said it's working with outside investigators to understand the scale of the breach.
articles.body:
Cybersecurity and automation giant Infoblox has confirmed a cybersecurity incident, during which hackers accessed company information through one of its technology vendors.

Infoblox is a privately held cyber giant that provides companies cybersecurity and networking services, such as domain name resolution and identity and user access management.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Infoblox told TechCrunch that the company is “investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor.”

“We immediately activated our incident response procedures, took steps to contain the incident and are working with leading outside cybersecurity experts to investigate the facts, understand the scope and address any confirmed risks.”

TechCrunch has learned that the data breach involves a vendor that provides SharePoint data migration services, according to a notification sent by Infoblox about the breach, two people with knowledge of the incident told TechCrunch.

One of the people said sensitive customer data was taken in the breach.

According to public internet records seen by TechCrunch, Infoblox hosts much of its files, emails, and infrastructure with Microsoft, including a SharePoint server, which TechCrunch confirmed is accessible through Infoblox’s single sign-on provider. SharePoint is web-based software that companies use to share and host internal files and documents.

Infoblox has not named the third-party migration vendor that was hacked, but one person with knowledge of the incident said that Infoblox has terminated its work with the vendor.

The company’s spokesperson did not comment on this, but added that the company has “no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved” in the breach.

Infoblox would not say how many customers were affected by the incident, or if the company is aware at this time. The company also did not say, when asked, if it had been contacted by the hackers and if they had made any demands.

articles.title: Duffy seeks more FAA funding, but lawmakers want answers first
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is calling on Congress to approve $50 billion in emergency funding to upgrade the nation’s air traffic control (ATC) technology after a rare nationwide ground stop led to the cancellation of 17,000 flights over the weekend. But Democratic lawmakers are arguing the Trump administration hasn’t fully justified or explained the need…
articles.body:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is calling on Congress to approve $50 billion in emergency funding to upgrade the nation’s air traffic control (ATC) technology after a rare nationwide ground stop led to the cancellation of 17,000 flights over the weekend.

But Democratic lawmakers are arguing the Trump administration hasn’t fully justified or explained the need for the funds, with many calling for a comprehensive investigation into what caused the hours-long ground stop first.

Republicans in Congress already allocated $12.5 billion to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) in July 2025 via the One Big Beautiful Bill Act . Now, their Democratic counterparts are asking where that money went.

During an impromptu White House press conference late Friday night and multiple TV interviews over the weekend, Duffy repeated his request for additional FAA funding from lawmakers.

“This is the most bipartisan idea in Washington right now, because everyone agrees to it. And when everyone agrees, shouldn’t we then take action? Let’s pass a bill and give us the resources to finish this job,” he said Sunday on CNN’s “ State of the Union .”

President Trump backed up his Transportation secretary on Sunday, saying the requested money for ATC is “desperately needed” to upgrade an outdated system.

“We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs,” he wrote Sunday on Truth Social . “Congress must approve.”

The president said Monday that he takes no responsibility for the failing systems.

“I think the one good thing that comes out of it — I’m sure Congress now will give us the money to pay,” Trump told reporters.

The spending and tax legislation GOP lawmakers passed last year designated billions to the FAA for replacing aging radar systems, telecommunications and traffic control centers, along with modernizing ATC towers and boosting recruitment of controllers.

But Duffy had asked for an additional $30 billion for the agency throughout this year. After Friday’s catastrophe, he upped his request by $20 billion.

“This is an emergency. I want Congress to give us emergency funding. This is bipartisan, this is American. I want $50 billion,” he told reporters in the White House briefing room.

The Modern Skies Act, which Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) and Rep. Tracey Mann (R-Kan.) introduced earlier this fall, calls for $10.1 billion for ATC modernization and $10 billion in improvements to terminals and ATC towers — part of $30 billion in total proposed funding.

The legislation has the support of industry stakeholders, with Schmitt saying Sunday the Senate must “ take it up immediately .”

But Democrats are throwing the challenge flag, blasting the administration for asking for more funding when it has yet to utilize already-allocated dollars.

“Our air traffic controllers have been failed by Secretary Duffy,” Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.) wrote Sunday on the social platform X.

DeLauro, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, equated Duffy’s $50 billion funding request to a “ransom with no plan,” saying previously appropriated FAA funds “sat largely unspent.”

Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), the ranking member on the Senate Commerce subcommittee on aviation, wrote Friday on X she will be “ demanding answers ” from the FAA regarding the ground stop.

Then on Monday, the Illinois Democrat pushed back on Duffy telling CNBC the FAA can build a new telecommunications system “quickly” if Congress provides the necessary funding.

“We don’t need to just ‘build it quickly.’ We need to build it safely,” Duckworth wrote on X .

Yet Nick Daniels, the president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, argued additional funding is necessary to upgrade the FAA’s automation platform.

Such an upgrade, he said, would merge two separate systems into a “common” platform that would “integrate” information for controllers.

“It’s almost like having a PlayStation 1 try to talk to a Game Boy. It’s just two different type[s] of technologies,” Daniels said of the status quo.

“They know, just like we know, the investment is needed more than ever if we’re going to keep up with the next demands of aviation in the U.S. and remain the world standard for it,” Daniels added, referring to lawmakers.

Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, said he doesn’t see Congress acting until they get a “very detailed” plan showing why more money is needed and what has happened with the previous money from the president’s One Big Beautiful Bill.

The incident is the first major crisis the federal government has faced since Republicans lost big in the midterm elections earlier this month, and some have criticized the administration’s response.

“It was more of a missed opportunity for the president to step up and show some leadership,” Doug Heye, a Republican strategist, said. “Instead, he was absent.”

West said Trump should’ve been at the Friday evening press conference “just to reassure people that things were under control and the situation was not going to become even more negative.”

At Friday’s briefing, only Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Duffy were present. Mullin credited Trump’s leadership for how the team he put together was handling the crisis.

Shannon A. Bowen, a professor at the University of South Carolina who studies ethics and futurism in the strategic communication discipline and practice, said Duffy and Mullin’s press conference was “quite calculated on the president’s part to let his Cabinet members take the heat of the initial questions … and the initial response.”

“I do think, however, it’s always going to be something that the president should weigh in when you have a national level crisis type of response,” she said. “So, it probably would have provided some comfort to people stranded at airports to hear at least the president saying, ‘We care … we know you’re stranded, we’re working on this as quickly as we can to get the problem resolved.’”

articles.title: Buttigieg fires back at Trump over FAA outage blame
articles.summary: Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg on Monday went after President Trump for blaming him for the recent Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop. “Well, we’ve been trying to get the money for two years to fix it, and Buttigieg ruined the system,” Trump told reporters Monday outside the White House discussing the air traffic control…
articles.body:
Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg on Monday went after President Trump for blaming him for the recent Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop.

“Well, we’ve been trying to get the money for two years to fix it, and Buttigieg ruined the system,” Trump told reporters Monday outside the White House discussing the air traffic control system. “He totally ruined it. The Democrats — really — it’s very old, but what they did really set back the system a long way.”

In a post on the social platform X Monday afternoon , Buttigieg said, “As secretary, I made sure to leave air travel in better condition than when we arrived.”

“We reversed a decade of decline in air traffic controller staffing, drove down runway safety incidents, and when I left office we were experiencing the lowest flight cancellation rates in years,” he added.

“As part of that work, I launched a project to transition the FAA’s communications system from copper wire to a modern network,” the former Transportation secretary added. “I am glad the Trump administration has continued that work, but they have so far failed to explain why their execution of it triggered the worst FAA communications breakdown this century.”

Trump also said Monday that he didn’t accept any responsibility for the FAA’s nationwide ground stop the prior week. He instead pointed to old equipment and past administrations as behind the pause.

“I don’t take any responsibility,” Trump told reporters. “They did a great job — [Transportation] Secretary [Sean] Duffy — they acted incredibly. Everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt. No crashes. No nothing.”

“And I mean, the only responsibility should be for 40 years they should have done this,” he continued.

On Sunday, the agency said that preliminary findings point to a router at a radio facility in El Dorado, Ark., and an Amarillo, Texas-based radio site, both seen as causes for excessive data that flooded systems. The FAA was prompted by problems at both sites to take them both offline. An increasing rate of connections caused widespread failures, resulting in the ground stop, per The New York Times.

articles.title: Tech leaders are convinced that Jensen Huang’s exit was a plot against him
articles.summary: David Sacks, Tim Sweeney, and other prominent leaders in tech are raising questions about Jensen Huang’s departure as the CEO of Nvidia, theorizing that it was part of a bigger plot against him.
articles.body: Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation from Nvidia after more than 33 years has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry. Now prominent figures are calling for Huang’s reinstatement, and many are also hopping on board with a theory spreading throughout Silicon Valley: that the scandal is the result of a plot against the former CEO. At the center of this theory is the reporting from The New York Times that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, one of multiple women Huang is accused of having an affair with, is a Chinese spy. US agencies haven’t confirmed whether this is the case, and President Donald Trump claims he was unaware of any spy allegations. Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang set off the events that led to his resignation; subsequent reporting suggested he had an affair with two employees at Nvidia, including one of his direct reports. The revelation raised new questions around whether Nvidia customers, including Megaspeed, were funneling chips to China in circumvention of export restrictions. Last year, Nvidia intervened in a chip-smuggling probe surrounding the Singapore-based company, according to Bloomberg. David Sacks, a venture capitalist and former White House AI crypto advisor, has made it clear that he’s skeptical about The New York Times’ reporting. In a post on X, Sacks points to an article from CNN, which says US officials still can’t confirm that Alice Huang was a spy. “The spy narrative is collapsing already,” Sacks writes. He continued to question the spy allegations during Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event on Monday, saying: “The reason why Jensen lost his job is because of this lurid Chinese spy allegation. So if no one’s willing to back that up now, then again, I question why this entire chain of events happened.” Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney similarly expressed concern about how Huang’s resignation played out. In a reply to Sacks’ post about the CNN article, Sweeney said, “What?! So journalists with sketchy motives portrayed rumors from god-knows-who (lobbyists?) as facts sourced from intelligence officials and gaslit the NVIDIA board to push out the founder, CEO, and once-in-generation visionary?” Amjad Masad, the CEO of the AI app and website builder Replit, called the timing of Huang’s resignation “suspicious,” adding that “if Jensen, the premier champion of open models, is taken out then anyone who wants AI closed, centralized, and controlled might benefit.” SemiAnalysis, a research and consulting firm for the semiconductor and AI industry, posted a “conspiracy theory take on the situation,” speculating that Huang’s removal is a way to “remove opposition to an extremely hawkish China export control bill,” referring to the Remote Access Security Act (RASA). The bill, which Huang opposed, would extend AI export controls to cloud servers that allow companies in restricted countries to rent access to Nvidia’s AI chips. The Department of Commerce released an interim final rule on Monday in an attempt to address this loophole. More than 185,000 people, including Sweeney, Masad, Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, have signed a “Stand with Jensen” letter, calling for his reinstatement as CEO. The letter similarly calls for a closer look into the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy,” the letter says. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership. The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed.”

articles.title: United Airlines says system outage resolved
articles.summary: United Airlines on Monday said a system outage has been resolved, an issue that comes days after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a ground stop that heavily impacted the airline’s services. United told The Hill that it had “resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures” but that there was “no impact on flights…
articles.body:
United Airlines on Monday said a system outage has been resolved, an issue that comes days after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a ground stop that heavily impacted the airline’s services.

United told The Hill that it had “resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures” but that there was “no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights.”

“There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue,” the airline continued.

When questioned about the outage on social media , United said it was aware of a “widespread system outage” and it was “working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible.”

This comes after Friday’s nationwide ground stop caused flights across the country to be cancelled or delayed for several hours on Friday. It was only the third such stoppage in U.S. history, and its effects still were being felt days later.

United wrote on Sunday that most of its flights “this weekend are operating normally following” the ground stop but “some flights will continue to be delayed or canceled as we work to restore our aircraft and crew schedules.”

“Safety is our highest priority, and we’re grateful for the extraordinary work of our employees and your continued patience,” it added.

FAA officials indicated that preliminary findings pointed to a router at an Arkansas radio facility and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas as reasons for the excessive data flooding the systems, which was behind the nationwide ground stop.

Issues at both sites prompted the FAA to take them both offline, but a soaring rate of connections caused widespread failures, leading to the ground stop, The New York Times reported.

More than 10,000 flights within, into or out of the United States were delayed Sunday, and more than 2,300 were canceled, according to the flight-tracking website FlightAware . The incident marked the third nationwide grund stop, following a 90-minute outage in 2023 and on Sept. 11, 2001.

3rd aircraft carrier arrives in Middle East as Trump weighs Iran options

A third U.S. aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, bringing more U.S. service members and firepower, as President Trump weighs his options against Iran.

© Seaman Ryan Holloway/U.S. Navy, via AP

The U S S Theodore Roosevelt, a Nimitz-class, nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, with an embarked air wing of F/A-18E/F Super Hornets and EA-18G Growlers electronic warfare aircraft, is currently operating in the U.S. Central Command (Centcom) area of responsibility, the military confirmed on Monday.

Roosevelt joins USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, marking the second time this year the Pentagon has had three aircraft carriers in the Middle East.

USS George H.W. Bush arrived in the Centcom region in April. USS George Washington got there in August, joining a fleet of Navy destroyers, cruisers and littoral combat ships , which are helping to enforce the U.S. naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz.

The U.S. military has over 50,000 service member s in the Centcom area.

The Roosevelt’s arrival comes after Trump recently said the conflict, which began in late February has dragged on for over eight months, is “effectively over, ” but the president has not ruled out restarting major combat operations.

Trump said last week that the U.S. military is closely watching Pickaxe Mountain , a heavily fortified, deep underground Iranian nuclear and centrifuge-assembly complex located south of Natanz.

At the same time, the president has said that the U.S. does not need a deal with Iran and has informed Vice President Vance to shift from focusing on Iran talks to the administration’s anti-fraud agenda.

After meeting with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani a week ago, the president said U.S. regional allies prefer the continuation of the naval blockad e.

“We have the greatest military blockade ever. We have the new Iron Gate,” Trump said.

“Iron Gate is land, so by land and by sea and we will take care of business.”

articles.title: America’s biggest bank JPMorgan reveals software bug behind US bank transaction delays, rules out cyberattack
articles.summary: America’s largest bank JPMorgan Chase has now revealed that the temporary software bug led to the delays in some customer transactions on November 16,
articles.body: America’s largest bank JPMorgan Chase has now revealed that the temporary software bug led to the delays in some customer transactions on November 16, disrupting some consumer banking services and triggering reports of outages across parts of the US banking system. According to a report by CNBC, the bank stated that the issue was linked to a software bug in its on-premise hardware systems, resulting in some transactions taking longer than usual process. The lender also stressed that the customers were still able to access their accounts and funds and said that there was no evidence that the disruption was related to any cyber attack.Bank rules out wider systemic problemWhile outage reports surfaced across several major US banks, JPMorgan said the issue was not systemic. The bank noted that other financial institutions could experience slower transactions only if they were involved in payments or transfers with JPMorgan, meaning any knock-on effects were linked to interactions with the bank's systems rather than a broader banking-sector outage. CNBC reported that there was no indication that bad actors were involved in the incident and no sign that a common software bug was simultaneously affecting multiple banks“There is no evidence it is cyber-related,” a JPMorgan spokesperson said in a statement to CNBC. “This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” the spokesperson said. “We’re working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today.”Customers of Bank of America, Chase, JP Morgan report issues accessing accounts onlineCustomers across several of the largest banks in US ran into trouble trying to access their accounts online on Monday (November 17). According to outage tracking website Downdetector.com, users reported that services were down or experiencing issues across multiple major financial institutions and payment platforms, including Bank of America, Chase, JP Morgan, US Bank, Wells Fargo and Zelle. As per a report by AP, some Chase users trying to log in were met with an error notice stating: “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”Third tech outage in a weekThe problems follow major outages last week, when a Microsoft email outage disrupted businesses. Coverage also notes that a FAA outage halted commercial air traffic, making the bank problems the third major tech disruption in days.
